title: Does digital transformation improve the supply chain resilience?
Note on Stochastic Vehicle Routing With Delivery Choice Under Recourse Options
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  In this paper, we consider the stochastic vehicle routing problem with delivery choice, where, upon reaching a particular customer, the driver has the choice of how much to deliver once the customer demand is revealed. In our earlier work, a basic version of the problem was considered, in which the driver cannot return to the depot midway in a route to replenish the cargo on board (see Venkateshan and Mathur 2025). In the present work, we expand on the choices that the driver has by allowing the driver to return to the depot to replenish before returning to the same customer or to proceed to the next customer. We prove the optimality of different threshold‐based fulfillment policies. Tests show that these policies significantly reduce the computational effort needed to determine the optimal fulfillment policy along a route, as well as its associated expected profit. We also show that a single‐vehicle tour that visits all customers is optimal even if multiple vehicles are allowed.

title: Exact Solution of Picker Routing Problems in Zoned Warehouses With Scattered Storage
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  We present two picker routing problems in a warehouse split into multiple disjoint zones with a picker assigned to each zone. Scattered storage is applied, meaning an article can be stored at several pick positions in one or more zones, and capacity restrictions limit the number of collected articles for each picker. Both problems seek picker tours that collect all requested articles, with each tour operating within one zone. While the multi‐zone picker routing problem (MZPRP) minimizes the total length of all picker tours, the balanced multi‐zone picker routing problem (BMZPRP) balances the tour lengths by minimizing the length of the longest picker tour. Both problems constitute a three‐level optimization problem. While on the higher levels, zone assignment decisions and the selection of pick positions must be made, on the lower level, picker tours for each zone are determined. To solve both problems, we use a network‐flow model with covering constraints and varying objectives. This type of model was recently presented for the single picker routing problem with scattered storage, building on an extended state space of the dynamic‐programming approach by Ratliff and Rosenthal. Our model contains a network for each zone, and demand‐covering constraints across all zones ensure that the requested articles are collected. Computational experiments, including large instances with up to 200 articles, show that our solution approach efficiently solves the two problems within (milli‐)seconds. An analysis of the number of zones demonstrates that in larger warehouse layouts, zoning reduces routing costs compared to single‐zone picker routing.

title: Sharp proximity for group-labeled matroid bases
abstract: Let the elements of a matroid be labeled in an abelian group, and let \(F\) be a finite set of forbidden basis-label sums. We prove that, for every representable matroid, every basis is within \(|F|\) exchanges of an \(F\)-avoiding basis whenever one exists. This resolves the unweighted proximity conjecture for representable matroids over arbitrary fields, ... Read more

title: Second-Moment Stochastic Approximation Methods
abstract: Classical stochastic approximation methods rely on estimators of the first moment (mean) of a random regression function. We study methods that employ estimators of both the first and the second moments, which include modern deep-learning optimizers such as Adam and Muon as special cases. We derive second-moment stochastic approximation methods through the lens of optimal ... Read more

title: Digital Forensic Analysis of a Case of Pornographic Content Dissemination on WhatsApp Using the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Method
abstract: The dissemination of pornographic content through instant messaging applications such as WhatsApp is becoming increasingly widespread. A major obstacle to establishing legal proof in these cases is that perpetrators frequently use the "Delete for Everyone" feature to eliminate digital evidence. This study aims to apply the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) method to obtain digital artifacts from messages deleted on the perpetrator's device. A simulated scenario was conducted between the victim's device (Xiaomi Redmi 10C) and the perpetrator's device (a rooted Xiaomi Redmi S2). The investigation used MOBILedit Forensic Express for physical acquisition and Belkasoft Evidence Center for data analysis. The results show that the NIST framework successfully overcame anti-forensic obstacles. The recovered digital evidence included metadata from 3 deleted text messages with logical deletion status, 3 image files containing pornographic content (.tmp/.jpeg), and 2 video files (.mp4). Cross-validation between fragments from the perpetrator's msgstore.db database and the victim's screenshots demonstrates that this method can produce legally valid and compelling electronic evidence for court proceedings.

title: Principles of Good Scientific Practice in Geoinformatics: From Data Management to Reproducible Code
abstract: Principles of Good Scientific Practice in Geoinformatics: From Data Management to Reproducible Code Trial lecture (Probevorlesung, § 13 HabilO) for the Venia Legendi in Geovisual Analytics at the Faculty of Environmental Sciences, Technische Universität Dresden (October 15, 2026, Dresden, Germany). Reflecting the core principles discussed, this lecture and its underlying pipeline are openly archived as a version-controlled, persistent resource to demonstrate reproducible scientific practice in action. Abstract Spatial data science occupies a uniquely vulnerable position in the ongoing reproducibility crisis. Below high-level Python libraries lies a complex stack of compiled C/C++ system libraries (GDAL, GEOS, PROJ) where unannounced datum shifts or compiler updates silently alter coordinates without throwing errors. Concurrently, spatial planning practice frequently relies on GUI-based desktop GIS workflows and binary office documents (`.docx`), leaving zero audit trail for legal scrutiny or scientific verification. Grounded in the normative framework of the DFG Code of Conduct (Guidelines 7, 10, 11, and 12) and Mayer's principles of multimedia learning, this lecture outlines four foundational pillars to transition from fragile ad-hoc scripts to resilient, verifiable scholarship: Part I • Diagnose (The Reality Check): Identifying the root failure modes of spatial data science—from the "spatial curse" of compiled system dependencies and unrecorded point-and-click operations to the administrative friction of managing 22,000+ data cells across municipal Word documents. Part II • Structure (The Resilient Archive): Establishing core architectural principles: Separation of Concerns (SoC), Single Source of Truth (SSOT), and Knowledge Longevity. Demonstrating that tools (Typora, QGIS, Zotero) are merely disposable viewing lenses, whereas disciplined plain text (Markdown) and open formats (GeoPackage, GeoParquet) constitute the permanent archive of thought. Addressing the FAIR vs. ELSA dilemma through synthetic twins and probabilistic hashing. Part III • Construct (Freezing the Computation): Demonstrating parameterized, headless GIS batch pipelines. Using an authentic planning case study (1,500 wind turbine viewsheds calculated via headless GRASS GIS inside JupyterLab for regional planning), the lecture illustrates literate provenance, isolated Docker container layering (Carto-Lab), and automated GitLab CI/CD release pipelines. Part IV • Evaluate (The Generative Frontier): Governing the integration of non-deterministic Large Language Models (LLMs). Establishing Prompts as Code and conversational lineage archiving to maintain human-in-the-loop accountability, separating probabilistic model outputs from verifiable scientific scholarship. The lecture concludes with a pragmatic survival checklist for Master's theses and frames Good Scientific Practice through the lens of Calm Technology: disciplined conventions do not add administrative burden - they liberate researchers from technical friction to focus on intellectual synthesis. Artifacts in this Deposit `presentation.pdf`: Vector slide export rendered directly from the web presentation viewport. `presentation_source.zip`: Complete source repository containing Reveal.js Markdown files, assets, custom CSS, and interactive case study submodules. --- DFG Code of Conduct (Leitlinien zur Sicherung guter wissenschaftlicher Praxis): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14281892

title: Aplikasi Absensi Berbasis Android untuk Optimalisasi Pengelolaan Kehadiran Petugas Kebun Desa Hameli Ate
abstract: Attendance management for field-based garden workers requires a mechanism that integrates user identity, attendance time, and location in an accurate and easily monitored process. Manual attendance recording may cause delays in data recapitulation, difficulties in tracing attendance records, and limitations in validating employee locations. This study aims to develop an Android-based attendance application to optimize attendance management for garden workers in Hameli Ate Village. The system was developed using the Waterfall model, consisting of requirements analysis, system design, implementation, testing, and maintenance. Flutter was used as the frontend, Laravel as the backend API, MySQL as the database, and GPS/geolocation as the mechanism for validating workers’ positions based on predefined workplace coordinates and radius. The application provides login, check-in and check-out attendance, attendance history, leave and permission requests, monitoring, workplace location management, holiday management, and attendance reporting features. Functional testing was designed using Black Box Testing, while usability evaluation was planned using the System Usability Scale (SUS). The development results indicate that the system accommodates the main requirements of both workers and administrators and provides centralized attendance data management. However, actual testing data and SUS scores from real users were not yet available; therefore, the system’s quantitative success rate and usability level cannot yet be conclusively reported.

title: Agentic Synthesis of Open-Source Biomedical Repositories and Clinical Literature into Interactive Diagnostic & Medical Learning Tools for Low-Resource Healthcare Settings
abstract: Frontline community health workers (CHWs) and rural clinics in low-resource settings—particularly across underserved municipalities in South Asia and rural regions of the United States—face a severe clinical knowledge bottleneck. While peer-reviewed biomedical literature, genomic variant databases, and open-source clinical calculators expand exponentially, these resources remain fragmented across unstructured texts and incompatible software repositories that require high-bandwidth connectivity and specialized bioinformatics literacy. This research protocol introduces **`gwf-clinical-synthesis`**, a non-commercial, computational dry-lab framework developed at GoWithFund Inc. Leveraging long-context multi-agent reasoning in **Google Antigravity** powered by **Gemini 4 Argon** (1M-token unified context window) and the **Google DeepMind (GDM) Science Skills** ecosystem, our pipeline orchestrates parallel literature retrieval across PubMed/NCBI Entrez, OpenAlex, ClinVar, and ChEMBL, fuses fragmented open-source clinical simulation repositories into lightweight offline-capable web applications, and executes automated multi-agent citation-verification loops to eliminate large language model (LLM) hallucinations. Concurrently, we integrate geospatial and socio-economic vulnerability indicators via AlphaEarth Foundations to model optimal healthcare resource allocation across high-burden districts. All resulting datasets, verification benchmarks, and interactive medical learning modules are released open-source under Apache 2.0 and CC BY 4.0 licenses.

title: OpenAQ Python SDK
abstract: The OpenAQ Python SDK is the official Python client for interacting with the OpenAQ API. Compatible with Python ≥3.10, it is recommended over hand-written API access code, offering built-in best practices and features including: comprehensive type annotations with inline documentation for better IDE autocomplete; robust API validation with automatic checking of path and query parameters and clear, actionable error messages; deserialized response classes providing Python objects with attribute access, plus JSON and dictionary representation options; and automatic rate-limiting with expressive error handling that gracefully manages API limits.

title: ID-10-T: An Observational Case Study of Legacy Technical-Support Humour, Diagnostic Ambiguity, and Human–Computer Interface Failure
abstract: **ID-10-T: An Observational Case Study of Legacy Technical-Support Humour, Diagnostic Ambiguity, and Human–Computer Interface Failure** This dataset documents a humorous encounter between legacy technical-support folklore and a contemporary Linux gaming livestream. During a broadcast involving CachyOS, NVIDIA graphics hardware, Moonlight and Apollo, a viewer introduced the classic "ID-10-T Error" into the livestream chat. The contributor reports that the broadcaster subsequently asked what the error meant. The expression "ID-10-T" is a long-established technical-support joke which, when written without hyphens, produces "ID10T", visually resembling the word "IDIOT". It is not a genuine software, hardware or operating-system diagnostic. **Research objectives:** - Document the appearance of historical technical-support humour in contemporary computing environments.- Examine diagnostic ambiguity when fictional error codes resemble legitimate technical terminology.- Preserve a reproducible example of digital folklore and humour transmission.- Demonstrate evidence-based documentation of informal online interactions.- Distinguish observable evidence, reported dialogue and satirical interpretation. **Dataset contents:** The public archive contains structured CSV annotations, machine-readable JSON metadata, a methodological description, an evidence codebook, provenance records, SHA-256 integrity checksums, rights documentation and an explicitly satirical technical incident report. The underlying source excerpt is approximately 37.35 seconds long, recorded at 1920 × 1080 resolution and 60 frames per second. The original video is not redistributed because third-party publication rights have not been established. **Research limitations:** This is an exploratory, single-case observational dataset (N=1). The reported verbal reaction has not been independently transcribed, and the observation cannot establish causal relationships, statistical generalisations or conclusions about an individual's technical competence. The dataset combines genuine archival documentation with explicitly identified humour, demonstrating that even an absurd technical-support joke can be recorded using transparent methods, provenance tracking and reproducible research practices. **Conclusion:** The error code was fictional. The observation was real. The joke remains backward compatible.

title: Competition for Customer Attention is Creating Oversupply Pockets in US Micromobility
abstract: We present analytical and empirical arguments that competition over a nearly homogeneous service forces operators to oversupply scooters in urban centers. First, using deployment and ride data from operator APIs and city transportation departments, as well as telemetry data from one of the top three U.S. operators, we estimate average daily scooter utilization across nine major U.S. cities at 3.9%—half the 7.7% minimum utilization target set by transportation departments. Second, using a parsimonious game-theoretic model, we argue that if riders choose among available scooters roughly at random (e.g., the closest one), then in equilibrium all operators need to inflate their fleet sizes to preserve their market shares. Third, using granular data on riders’ choice sets and choices from Kansas City, MO, we provide evidence that these choices are indeed roughly random. Fourth, using our structurally estimated game-theoretic model, we find that in Kansas City, MO: (i) there is a 406% oversupply of scooters, (ii) the interaction between rider choice and competition accounts for 81% of this oversupply, and (iii) if the transportation department issued one more operator permit, oversupply would increase by an additional 82 pp. We conclude that transportation departments should be frugal with the number of permits they issue, and should welcome the consolidation of the scooter market.

title: Learning Optimal Classification Trees Robust to Distribution Shifts
abstract: We consider the problem of learning classification trees that are robust to distribution shifts between training and testing/deployment data. This problem arises frequently in high stakes settings such as public health and social work where data is often collected using self-reported surveys which are highly sensitive to e.g., the framing of the questions, the time when and place where the survey is conducted, and the level of comfort the interviewee has in sharing information with the interviewer. We propose a method for learning optimal robust classification trees based on mixed-integer robust optimization technology. In particular, we demonstrate that the problem of learning an optimal robust tree can be cast as a single-stage mixed-integer robust optimization problem with a highly nonlinear and discontinuous objective. We reformulate this problem equivalently as a two-stage linear robust optimization problem for which we devise a tailored solution procedure based on constraint generation. We evaluate the performance of our approach on numerous publicly available datasets, and compare the performance to a regularized, non-robust optimal tree. We show an increase of up to 12.48 percentage points in worst-case accuracy and of up to 4.85 percentage points in average-case accuracy across several datasets and distribution shifts from using our robust solution in comparison to the non-robust one.

title: Stochastic Dual Dynamic Programming for Log-linear Autoregressive Uncertainty in the Right-hand Side
abstract: We consider the generation of cuts in stochastic dual dynamic programming (SDDP) for multistage stochastic linear programming problems with stagewise dependent uncertainty in the right-hand side described by a nonlinear autoregressive process. We first derive cut formulas for the general nonlinear autoregressive process. For these general cuts, the computational tractability becomes a major challenge for SDDP-type algorithms. We are, however, able to develop tractable closed-form cut formulas for the special case of log-linear autoregressive processes. The obtained cuts are in general non-convex in the history of the stochastic process, but still linear in all decision variables, and thus can be directly incorporated into the subproblems in SDDP without compromising their linearity. If solvers do not allow for this, our formulas can be used to adapt the intercept of a given cut to a scenario at hand in a computationally tractable way. In this sense, cuts generated for one specific scenario are shared with other scenarios. Our findings are supported by a computational study of a hydrothermal scheduling problem, which demonstrates a favorable performance of our proposed version of SDDP compared to approaches from the literature.

title: Impact in 2025
authors: Consortium of European Social Science Data Archives
abstract: The Consortium of European Social Science Data Archives (CESSDA ERIC) is a distributed research infrastructure that operates through a network of 22 Service Providers and 12 partners across Europe. In 2025, the consortium worked collectively to deliver on its strategic priorities: Data, People, and Landscape. It preserved, curated, and archived 46,000 primary digital objects, including datasets, that were downloaded or viewed 793,000 times. It supported 842,000 publications, of which an estimated 40% were peer-reviewed publications. It engaged over 14,000 participants in 558 training events. By preserving and enabling the reuse of social science data, this brief highlights how CESSDA has turned public investments in data collection into long-term data assets for research, policy, and society.

title: Systemically Important Banks and Loan Performance: Evidence from India
abstract:
We examine whether designating banks as systemically important affects loan performance in an emerging-market setting where such banks are large domestic institutions and market imperfections make monitoring crucial for loan performance. Using loan-level data and the staggered designation of banks as Domestic Systemically Important Banks (DSIBs) in India, we find that loan performance deteriorates following DSIB designation. The evidence points to bank-level moral hazard as the underlying mechanism: DSIBs reduce postorigination monitoring and weaken loan recovery efforts. Borrowers respond accordingly, exhibiting poorer financial health and loan repayment, particularly on loans extended by DSIBs.
                  This paper was accepted by Jan Bouwens, accounting.
                  Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03238 .

title: Why Do We Discriminate? Directional Beliefs and Biased Information Processing
abstract:
Identifying the cause of discrimination is crucial to designing effective policies and to understanding discrimination dynamics. This paper provides a potential link between existing models of taste-based and statistical discrimination by studying directional belief formation through biased information search and processing. By selectively acquiring and processing information, individuals form directional beliefs and consequently discriminate based on these beliefs. Through a series of experiments in which individuals endogenously acquire and process various signals, I document discrimination stemming from directional beliefs and demonstrate important differences in how it manifests compared with taste-based and statistical discrimination. Finally, I show that limiting individuals’ scope to interpret information reduces such discrimination.
                  This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis.
                  Funding: Financial support from the Sustainable Architecture for Finance in Europe Experiment Center Frankfurt [Grant 232406], the Interdisciplinary Public Policy Mainz [Grant A2021011], and the Mainzer Wissenschaftsstiftung is gratefully acknowledged.
                  Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01818 .

title: AI-Driven Human Task Substitution: Evidence from Google Translate and ChatGPT
abstract:
We examine how different generations of artificial intelligence (AI) substitute for human knowledge worker tasks, leveraging two sequential natural experiments in the translation industry. We study the introduction of Google Neural Machine Translation (GNMT), a predictive, task-specific AI, as well as ChatGPT, a broad, general-purpose generative AI, in a major online labor market. Distinguishing between analytical tasks (regular translations) and intuitive tasks (transcreations, which require creative and cultural adaptation), we estimate difference-in-differences models on transaction-level data from 2016 to 2017 and 2022 to 2023. We find that GNMT reduced the demand for analytical tasks by economically meaningful magnitudes, while having no detectable effect on intuitive tasks. By contrast, ChatGPT produced substantially larger and more uniform reductions for both analytical and intuitive tasks, indicating a marked expansion in the scope and magnitude of AI substitution. By comparing these two technological shocks within the same labor market, we show that conclusions about which types of human work are resilient to automation do not straightforwardly generalize from predictive to generative AI.
                  This paper was accepted by Joshua Gans, business strategy.
                  Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06740 .

title: Operations management for sustainable development and public policy making
abstract: Public policy making often faces challenges in implementation due to a lack of attention to operational realities. Operations management (OM) research, with its strong empirical component and focus on detailed model-based mechanisms, offers unique insights for successful policy execution. This paper explores the synergies between economics, development economics, and OM in addressing public policy implementation, arguing that OM’s process-level understanding, empirical rigor, and focus on operational feasibility can enhance policy design and evaluation. We illustrate this potential through examples from sustainability and social development, demonstrating how OM can bridge the gap between economic policy insights and operational execution.

title: Machine Learning‐Assisted Optimization for Dynamic Supply Network Design in the Additive Manufacturing Platform
abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  Distributed manufacturing enabled by additive manufacturing (AM) allows supply chains to rapidly adapt to changing market conditions through flexible facility relocation and capacity adjustment. However, existing studies largely overlook the logistical aspects of AM‐based supply chains and typically treat facility location and logistics decisions separately. This study addresses this gap by developing a novel AM supply network design model that simultaneously considers the dynamic relocation of AM facilities, the adjustment of production capacities, and delivery routing decisions over multiple periods. We formulate the problem as a mixed‐integer linear programming model (MILP). Given the computational challenges associated with the delivery routing component, we propose a machine learning genetic algorithm (MLGA) approach to solve the problem efficiently. MLGA incorporates a machine learning surrogate to estimate the cost of the capacitated vehicle routing subproblem (CVRP), thereby significantly accelerating the convergence of the genetic algorithm (GA). We train two different machine learning surrogates: One based on a neural network model and the other on an XGBoost model. The MLGA solution methodology, under both surrogate models, performs satisfactorily in terms of solution quality and computation time across a set of randomly generated instances. Extensive sensitivity analyses are also conducted on a realistic use case to evaluate the model's applicability under varying service area, demand, and cost scenarios, offering valuable managerial insights and practical implications.

title: The quasi-convex Rockafellar theorem
abstract: Rockafellar showed that every cyclically monotone operator is contained in the subdifferential of a convex function, and characterized the maximal ones. We establish the quasi-convex analogue of this theorem, with no assumption on the operator: in any separable Banach space, a setting we show to be sharp, every cyclically quasi-monotone operator is contained in the normal cone operator of a quasi-convex function. In finite dimension, we characterize maximal cyclically quasi-monotone operators and show that they are maximal quasi-monotone. Unlike in the convex case, the potential is not unique, and we build it from a preference relation obtained through successive preorders. As applications, we extend Afriat's theorem on revealed preferences in economics to infinite data sets, and obtain Kantorovich-type potentials for a supremal optimal transport problem.

title: A Decomposition-Based Data-Driven Branch-and-Bound Approach for Black-Box Global Optimization
abstract: Many scientific and engineering applications require the global optimization of expensive black-box functions. In high-dimensional settings, however, achieving computational scalability is a major challenge. To address this challenge, we propose a distributed spatial branch-and-bound framework that exploits partially separable structure for the global optimization of box-constrained black-box problems. The proposed framework adopts a two-layer structure in which branching is performed only on a lower-dimensional set of coupling variables in an outer layer. Within each outer node, the remaining non-overlapping (private) variables, which appear independently across blocks, have their domains partitioned and explored in parallel within an inner layer, resulting in a naturally parallelizable framework that is well suited for implementation on multi-core CPU architectures. At each node, valid upper bounds are obtained via sampling, with optional refinement using a local solver, while lower bounds are computed using data-driven convex underestimators constructed over partitions of the private variables. A residual-based correction and finite-sample validity analysis provide conditions under which the partitionwise underestimators are valid lower bounds, while the proposed branching and refinement mechanism establishes convergence to an $ε$-global optimum. Numerical studies on benchmark and ODE-constrained parameter-estimation problems demonstrate improvements in both sampling efficiency and computational performance relative to monolithic approaches.

title: On the Complexity of Linear Programs with Parametric Constraint Matrices
abstract: While sensitivity analysis for linear programs with parametric right- hand side vectors is well established, cases involving parametric constraint matrices remain less explored. To address this gap, we investigate linear programs where the constraint matrix depends linearly on a scalar parameter. Our goal is to compute the minimum and maximum optimal values of these parametric linear programs within a fixed parameter range. This corresponds to solving two bilevel programs. We show that both decision versions of these optimization problems are NP-complete by proving both NP-hardness and membership in NP. We additionally identify three sufficient conditions on the parametric matrix under which the bilevel programs are no longer NP-hard. We introduce a reformulation for both problems, together with a Farkas-based certificate for the lower-level feasibility condition, and compare the execution time for solving them on standard benchmark instances. The experiments highlight a practical dichotomy. Although both bilevel optimizations are NP-hard, computing the parameter value corresponding to the minimum of the linear program is fast, whereas computing the value corresponding to the maximum is not. We relate this asymmetry to the parametric equality constraints, whose free dual variables leave the relaxation of the maximum reformulation unbounded.

title: Dual-Inertial Bregman Methods with Energy-Based Safeguarding
abstract: We develop a dual-inertial framework for convex optimization that introduces inertia in dual coordinates while retaining the Bregman proximal-type oracles. For unrestarted iterations, uniformly bounded positive directional variation gives a last-iterate $\cO((1+\log k)/k^2)$ rate, improving to $\cO(k^{-2})$ under additional weighted summability. A computable safeguarded algorithm gives a global $\cO(N^{-1})$ objective-gap bound for the best accepted point, where $N$ counts all proximal oracle calls. Under local strong-convexity and kernel regularity conditions, all three safeguarded methods restart finitely and attain a final-epoch last-iterate $\cO(N^{-2})$ rate. Numerical experiments compare objective accuracy and computational cost on entropy regression and nonnegative least squares. Comparative numerical experiments illustrate the performance advantages of the proposed methods.

title: Tracking a Small Set of Experts in Online Convex Optimization
abstract: For the fundamental problem of prediction from expert advice, Freund asked whether one could compete with a comparator that switches $k$ times among only $m$ experts. For a discrete set of experts, this problem was resolved by Bousquet and Warmuth (2020), who gave an efficient algorithm with optimal regret matching the information-theoretic limit.   We study the analogous problem in online convex optimization, where the action space is continuous. An inefficient algorithm can be derived by discretizing the action space and applying the Bousquet--Warmuth algorithm, giving regret of $\widetilde{O}(md+k)$, while the best known efficient algorithm for this problem has regret $\widetilde{O}(dk)$. We show that this computational inefficiency is inherent, establishing a separation between the information-theoretic and polynomial-time regret achievable for this problem. Specifically, under the hypergraphic planted-clique conjecture, we show that for every polynomial-time algorithm there exist instances for which it incurs at least $(k\sqrt d)^{1-o(1)}$ regret.

title: When Does Momentum Help in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards?
abstract: Momentum is a classical tool for accelerating convex optimization and a standard component of modern large language model training. Yet recent empirical work has questioned the usefulness of first-moment momentum in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We study this question through a bandit formulation of RLVR with bias-corrected exponential moving average (EMA) momentum, where the EMA coefficient $β$ controls how quickly the weights on past gradients decay. When policy gradients are evaluated exactly, we prove that increasing $β$ within a range that prevents overshoot strictly accelerates optimization. When gradients are estimated from sampled responses, a positive expected gain can be obscured by sampling fluctuations. We show that as the learning rate $η$ decreases, the expected gain with fixed $β$ vanishes faster than these fluctuations, whereas increasing $β$ to keep $η/(1-β)$ within the safe regime preserves a nonvanishing gain that eventually dominates them. Bandit simulations quantitatively validate these predictions. RLVR experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base using SGD with EMA and AdamW support our principle of choosing larger coefficients in practical LLM post-training. On Qwen2.5-32B with AdamW, simply increasing $β_1$ improves mean validation accuracy by nearly $2$ percentage points over the conventional choice, demonstrating the principle's effectiveness at a larger model scale.

title: On Partial Optimality in QUBO via Quadratic Posiform Autarkies
abstract: Partially optimal assignments (also called persistencies) allow combinatorial optimization problems to be reduced by fixing a subset of variables to values consistent with at least one optimal solution. For the quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem, such assignments can be computed efficiently via autarkies of quadratic posiforms. However, the largest autarky domain and thus the number of fixed variables can depend on the specific posiform representation. We show that every quadratic posiform with the greatest possible constant term (the roof-dual bound) yields the largest autarky domain obtainable from any quadratic posiform. By computing such a roof-dual-optimal quadratic posiform and a corresponding autarky with largest domain in polynomial time, one can therefore attain the maximum partial optimality obtainable by quadratic posiform autarkies in polynomial time. This justifies the computation of roof-dual-optimal quadratic posiforms and corresponding autarkies in popular polynomial-time algorithms and establishes that finding additional partial optimality in QUBO requires going beyond autarkies of quadratic posiforms.

title: Envelope Cubic Regularized Newton Method for Nonconvex-Strongly-Concave Minimax Optimization
abstract: We study nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax problem $\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_x}}\max_{\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_y}}f(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})$ in which the objective has $ρ$-Lipschitz Hessian and condition number $κ$. We propose envelope cubic regularized Newton method (ECRN) which applies a refined inexact cubic regularized Newton method to the envelope of the primal function $Φ(\cdot) : = \max_{\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_y}}f(\cdot,\mathbf{y})$. We show that ECRN finds approximate second-order stationary points of $Φ(\cdot)$ with $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrtρ\,κ^{3/4}\varepsilon^{-3/2})$ second-order oracles, improving the condition number dependence $\mathcal{O}(κ^{2})$ achieved by the best known second-order methods. Our improvement comes from the key observation that the Hessian Lipschitz parameter of the envelope is $\mathcal{O}(ρκ^{3/2})$, which is sharper than the order of $\mathcal{O}(ρκ^{3})$ for the function $Φ(\cdot)$. We also conduct a lower bound on second-order methods to show that our complexity is optimal up to a logarithmic factor.

title: Benign Degeneracy for First-Order Methods in Exact Boolean Moment-SOS Relaxations
abstract: Pseudo-Boolean optimization -- minimizing a polynomial over $\{\pm 1\}^n$ -- includes MAX-CUT, binary quadratic optimization, and Ising models. The moment-sum-of-squares (Moment-SOS) hierarchy provides certified semidefinite relaxations that are often empirically exact at low order. We ask: once a relaxation is exact, how difficult is the resulting semidefinite program (SDP) to solve with first-order methods?   Exactness does not imply regularity. At every order $d \ge 2$, a unique rank-one moment optimum is primal degenerate; moreover, if one optimal SOS certificate is strictly complementary, then the certificate set is positive-dimensional and contains singular boundary points. Thus first-order methods may converge to singular endpoints, around which pointwise analyses that assume regularity at the limit cannot establish a local linear convergence rate.   We show that, for exact Boolean Moment-SOS relaxations in their canonical quotient form, this degeneracy is nevertheless benign. We develop an abstract mechanism, which we call residual-field rigidity, that propagates regularity from the relative interior of the optimal set to its singular boundary. For Boolean Moment-SOS, unique rank-one exactness and the existence of one strictly complementary certificate suffice to trigger this mechanism, yielding a uniform error bound around the entire optimal set. Consequently, exact ADMM, exact sGS-ADMM, and fixed-step PDHG converge eventually linearly from every initialization, even when their limiting certificate is singular. Finally, outside a lower-dimensional semialgebraic exceptional set of Boolean objectives, these hypotheses hold simultaneously at every uniquely rank-one exact order.

title: Dimension-Optimal Dynamic Regret in Exp-Concave Online Learning
abstract: Tracking changing comparators is a central problem in online learning. For exp-concave losses, previous work established the $T^{1/3}P_T^{2/3}$ dependence on the horizon $T$ and Euclidean path length $P_T$ for fixed dimension, while the optimal cost of dimension remained unresolved. We resolve this question by establishing a sharp $d^{1/3}$ curved dimension factor, improving the $d^{2/3}$ factor of recent switching and interval reductions [1, 2]. To achieve this improvement, we develop a proper, full-information learner on compact convex subsets of $\mathbb{R}^d$ that adapts to the unknown path length and, under fixed dimension-independent diameter, gradient, and curvature parameters, guarantees   $$\operatorname{Reg}_T(u_{1:T}) \le \widetilde{O}\left(d+\min\left\{d^{1/3}T^{1/3}P_T^{2/3},\sqrt{TP_T},T\right\}\right).$$   A matching lower bound on a diameter-one Euclidean ball establishes the minimax frontier up to logarithmic factors when $T\gtrsim d^2$, including the transition from the curved rate to larger path budgets. The lower bound already holds for losses that depend on only one coordinate per round, isolating an unavoidable cost of learning across directions. Our upper bound follows from square-root Gaussian KL control of comparator movement and a cancellation argument that pays for history restarts. The curved learner maintains $O(\log^2 T)$ Gaussian states, uses one gradient per round, and runs in time near-linear in $T$ under a Mahalanobis-projection oracle.

title: Continuous-Time q-Learning with Nonsmooth Value Functions: a BSDE Approach
abstract: We study continuous-time q-learning for entropy-regularized diffusion control without assuming classical differentiability of the value function. Rewards and admissible policies need only be Borel measurable, which allows discontinuous rewards. The diffusion coefficient $σ$ is action independent and locally uniformly elliptic, and the drift is $b_0 + σψ$, with $b_0$ action independent and $ψ$ bounded. In this setting the q-function involves the value only through its gradient. For each admissible policy, we represent its value by a backward stochastic differential equation (BSDE) and prove that this value is continuous before the horizon, although the data are only measurable. Replacing the gradient with a measurable representation of the martingale integrand, we define the q-function up to Lebesgue-null sets and recover the classical definition when the value function is smooth. We then prove policy improvement, when the Gibbs update is admissible, and martingale characterizations of the value and the q-function from on-policy and off-policy observations. Here the candidate value need only be continuous before the horizon, and actions are sampled on a deterministic finite grid and held constant between sampling times. Under an integrability condition on the reward, we show that a second BSDE gives an upper bound for the optimal value, attained when its Gibbs policy is admissible, and we characterize its solution in the same way.

title: An Analytic 0.48-Approximation for Non-Monotone k-Submodular Maximization under a Matroid Constraint
abstract: We give a randomized polynomial-time $0.48$-approximation for maximizing a nonnegative non-monotone $k$-submodular function under a matroid constraint, for every $k\ge2$. The algorithm combines a top-two label rule with a nested-chain potential and maximum-weight matroid bases. Its analysis reduces the approximation guarantee to a one-dimensional time allocation: a uniform local lower bound leads to a linear differential equation, concavity closes the remaining interval, and two elementary budgets complete the proof. A strict saving in the time budget absorbs sampling and discretization errors, yielding the exact $0.48$ guarantee in the value-oracle model.

title: New Modelling and Solution Frameworks for Multiple Objectives, Decomposability and Impulsivity in Continuous-time Markov Decision Processes
abstract: Impulsive control, in the context of continuous-time Markov decision processes (CTMDPs), refers to actions that instantaneously update the state of the process, leading to theoretical complications. Previous work has overcome these complications, but at the expense of approachability and ease of implementation: those models are mathematically complex and incompatible with pre-existing solution methods. This paper presents an alternative formulation of impulsive control for CTMDPs that is easier to employ in the modelling of real-world problems and can be solved by pre-existing solution methods. This formulation is then extended to allow for multiple objectives and decomposability. A decomposition-based heuristic method is developed that leverages Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition to find approximate Pareto fronts for large multi-objective decomposable impulsive CTMDPs. The modelling framework and solution methodology are applied to a dynamic maintenance problem to demonstrate their computational efficiency, solution space coverage, and solution quality.

title: Routes planning in a condominium company using mathematical optimization
abstract: This work focuses on planning daily routes for a group of employees of a condominium company. Given a set of employees and a set of customers with pre-scheduled visits, we want to build doubly-open routes to guarantee visits to all customers, ensuring that each customer is visited by an employee with the appropriate skills to carry out the required activity. The travel times between customers and the service time in each customer are known. The problem includes time windows for visiting customers, each employee has a maximum working time, and the daily working period is between 9 AM and 6:30 PM. The routes respect the lunch break period if they extend from morning to afternoon, which means that lunch break can be avoided if the route is fully completed in the morning or in the afternoon. The aim is to minimize the distance covered by all routes with a penalty for including lunch breaks. The distances and times between customers are collected via an API to Microsoft Azure; and the solutions are then displayed on Bing Maps. The results obtained show the operational advantages of an efficient and effective vehicle routing planning in a specific condominium management company. The model can be extended to other service provider companies.

title: A particle swarm optimization with a reduced-subspace trust-region safeguard for contact-rich controller tuning
abstract: Contact-rich robotic insertion is challenging because uncertainty in alignment, friction, and contact conditions can lead to unsuccessful assembly, excessive contact forces, and jamming. Designing a reliable controller therefore requires balancing insertion performance, robustness, and recovery from unexpected contact. In this paper, we propose PSO+TR, a derivative-free optimization (DFO) method that combines the exploratory search of particle swarm optimization (PSO) with a trust-region (TR) procedure for local refinement to improve the search process when progress stagnates. We apply the method to derivative-free policy optimization of an interpretable robotic insertion controller, jointly tuning its motion, feedback, and recovery parameters while preserving its predefined control structure. The proposed approach is evaluated on 93 eligible benchmark problems from the bound-constrained programs (BCP) collection and a synthetic contact-rich planar insertion task under uncertain operating conditions. Three random seeds per benchmark problem yield 279 matched problem--seed instances per method. PSO+TR reaches the prescribed target on 228 of these instances (81.72\%), the highest observed target-attainment rate among the five compared methods, which also include PSO, randomized black-box optimization (VRBBO), matrix adaptation evolution strategy (MAES), and differential evolution (DE). Across eight robotic optimizer seeds, the deployed controller-selection pipeline achieves 97.78\% completion under development conditions and 58.00\% under withheld stress conditions, compared with 91.22\% and 31.12\%, respectively, for the fixed staged controller. The stress violation rate is reduced from 20.69\% to 2.19\%. These findings support combining global and local search for DFO and structured contact-rich controller tuning. The synthetic planar results require validation on physical robots.

title: Ergodic and Metastable Behavior of Stochastic Popularity Dynamics in Social Networks
abstract: This paper studies popularity dynamics in social networks, where users' engagement with competing channels is driven by intrinsic content quality, social influence, and popularity feedback. We introduce a stochastic model in which users interact through a directed influence network and channel exposure depends jointly on these three mechanisms. We first characterize the resulting dynamics in the absence of intrinsic quality, showing that popularity concentrates asymptotically on a single channel, leading to a winner-takes-all regime. When all channels have positive intrinsic quality, we establish ergodicity of the popularity process and characterize its long-run behavior. We further show that, when intrinsic quality is small, the system exhibits metastable behavior: it can remain for long periods near configurations dominated by a single channel before transitioning to another. These results highlight how weak quality differences can coexist with strong path dependence induced by popularity feedback. We then investigate platform-level interventions and propose controls that compensate for network-induced exposure biases and mitigate excessive concentration. Analytical results are illustrated through numerical simulations and an empirical analysis of YouTube data, whose observed popularity dynamics are consistent with the proposed stochastic framework. The results provide a mathematical framework for understanding the interplay between quality, social influence, and reinforcement in online popularity dynamics.

title: New spherical codes by tuning an annealing solver
abstract: The spherical code problem asks how to place $N$ points on a unit sphere in $D$ dimensions to maximize the smallest distance between two points. It is a non-smooth and non-convex max-min problem, where few problem sizes have known optimal solutions, some have constructions, but most still only have numerically obtained solutions. We use a simple solver, with seven parameters, that anneals a LogSumExp surrogate, minimizes with L-BFGS, applies a random perturbation between anneals, and repeats with no acceptance test until a fixed limit is reached. We search the solver parameters for every instance with $N \le 1024$, $3 \le D \le 32$, and $N > 2D$, a total of 29,670 instances, using 32 parameter trials. We then run the solver for 60 seconds with the best parameters for each instance, without utilizing any symmetries or existing solutions. After enforcing monotonicity of the results and numerically polishing the solutions, we improve the best known code in 4,577 instances. When a single set of solver parameters is used for all instances, with one 60-second episode, the number of improvements is still 3,649. From our records, we find 24 codes with an exact algebraic cosine. Among our ablations, we find that 1) the repeated anneal contributes most to improvements, 2) at our $32 \times 60$-second budget only fitting one parameter per-instance is better than fitting all seven, and 3) good parameters can be predicted from the instance size. We provide the solver code, the fitted parameters, and the codes.

title: L1 Minimum Energy Estimation of Positive Systems
abstract: We present a novel class of minimum energy estimation problems for positive linear systems with linear costs subject to coupled process and measurement disturbances, where the latter is bounded by the state and the former is bounded by the noise. Through dynamic programming we show that the problem admits explicit solutions. Remarkably, the Luenberger observer structure of the optimal estimator emerges from the optimization itself, with a switching gain that inherits the sparsity of the disturbance constraints, and it is obtained from a differential equation in the finite horizon case. In the infinite horizon case, an algebraic equation characterizes the limit of the finite-horizon solution and yields a stationary estimator with a static gain. We introduce two distinct notions of detectability to characterize when the static gain stabilizes the error dynamics while preserving their positivity, and analyze under which conditions the stationary solution can be formulated as a linear program. We further establish that a disturbance perturbation of finite L1-norm yields an estimation error of finite L1-norm. The framework is illustrated on a large-scale irrigation network.

title: Recursive Gradient Retraction Methods for Stochastic Nonconvex Optimization on Stiefel Manifolds
abstract: Nonconvex optimization on Stiefel manifolds underlies many problems in machine learning and deep learning. However, existing stochastic Riemannian retraction methods often rely on stepsizes that require prior knowledge of the gradient Lipschitz constant, a prescribed iteration horizon, or restrictive batch-size choices. We develop {\sf RGR}, a recursive gradient retraction method for stochastic nonconvex optimization on Stiefel manifolds. Instead of recursively updating gradient estimators in changing tangent spaces, {\sf RGR} constructs them in the Euclidean space and subsequently maps them to tangent space, thereby avoiding vector transport. The method comprises three variants: {\sf RGR-SPIDER} for finite-sum optimization and {\sf RGR-SRM} and {\sf RGR-EMA} for online stochastic optimization. {\sf RGR-SPIDER} is Lipschitz-free and horizon-free, as its adaptive stepsize requires neither prior knowledge of the gradient Lipschitz constant nor a prescribed iteration horizon. {\sf RGR-SRM} and {\sf RGR-EMA} are mini-batch and horizon-free methods whose convergence guarantees do not rely on prescribed large batch sizes and whose parameters can be chosen without prior knowledge of the total iteration budget. We show that {\sf RGR-SPIDER} reaches an $\varepsilon$-critical point using $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$ iterations and $\mathcal{O}(N+\sqrt{N}\varepsilon^{-2})$ component-gradient evaluations, where $N$ denotes the number of component functions. For the online setting, {\sf RGR-SRM} and {\sf RGR-EMA} achieve iteration complexities of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\varepsilon^{-3})$ and $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\varepsilon^{-4})$, respectively. Experiments on principal component analysis, low-rank matrix completion, and orthogonal convolutional neural networks demonstrate faster empirical convergence than methods that construct recursive gradient estimators directly in Riemannian tangent spaces.

title: On the Regularization of Primal-Dual Dynamics in Time-Dependent Nonconvex Optimization
abstract: We study continuous-time primal-dual dynamics for tracking solutions of time-dependent constrained optimization problems. First, for uniformly strongly convex-strongly concave saddle functions, we establish explicit finite-time tracking and additive-disturbance bounds. For convex problems, we then introduce a directional primal regularization, combined with dual Tikhonov regularization, and quantify the resulting optimization bias and constraint violation. For smooth nonconvex problems, we couple a proximal local convexification with a two-time-scale primal-dual flow and obtain a local tracking result under constraint qualification, second-order sufficiency, and temporal regularity. Numerical traffic-signal experiments at a single intersection evaluate the proposed method under vehicle-throughput and pedestrian-aware objectives, comparing it with standard signal-control schemes.

title: On the Optimisation Landscape of Overparameterised Weighted MMD
abstract: We study the optimisation landscape of the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) over weighted atomic measures. For the one-dimensional Gaussian kernel, we show that, for any compactly supported target distribution, sufficiently many particles ensure that every local minimum has arbitrarily small MMD. Moreover, any stationary point whose MMD remains bounded away from zero is unstable under an unweighted gradient flow over the particle locations. These results hold both when the weights are constrained to the simplex, and when they are unconstrained but optimised at each step. When the target is itself finitely supported, we further strengthen this result: beyond an explicit particle threshold, there are no spurious local minima, and every spurious stationary point is unstable. To our knowledge, these are the first finite-particle overparameterisation guarantees of their kind for weighted MMD optimisation.

title: ANOVA approximation for high-dimensional control systems
abstract: We study the data-driven approximation of control-affine systems, where the drift and each control vector field exhibit a low-dimensional structure. While the ANOVA (ANalysis Of VAriance) decomposition is tailored to low-dimensional structures, a straightforward implementation does not exploit control affinity, rendering the approximation computationally expensive. We propose a coupled least squares approach for given state-control samples, whose ansatz is affine linear in the control by construction and can be realized by a preprocessing of the ANOVA index sets. Based on a Marcinkiewicz--Zygmund inequality for the resulting ansatz space, we prove a probabilistic $L_2$-error bound with explicitly given constants. Separate error control on drift and input vector fields renders the approach flexible to, e.\,g., parameter changes. Finally, we numerically illustrate the identification of the coupling structure via global sensitivity indices on discretizations of a nonlinear advection-diffusion equation, the shallow water equations and the viscous Burgers equation.

title: Does Policy Mirror Descent Converge in Policy with Non-Decomposable Mirror Maps? A Counterexample
abstract: Policy mirror descent (PMD) refers to a class of policy optimization methods associated with different mirror maps. For a broad class of decomposable Legendre mirror maps encompassing many standard choices, Li and Wei [2026] show that the PMD policy sequence converges to an optimal policy from any admissible initialization under any positive constant step size, even when the optimal policy is not unique. In this note, we provide a counterexample with assistance from OpenAI's GPT-5.6 model, showing that PMD with a non-decomposable Legendre mirror map need not converge in policy.

title: GPU-Accelerated Preprocessing for Large-Scale Linear Programming
abstract: GPU-accelerated first-order methods are increasingly effective for solving large-scale linear programs (LPs), yet LP preprocessing remains predominantly CPU-based and can become costly. A key challenge is that dependencies among presolve reductions and frequent modifications to sparse LP data make efficient GPU parallelization difficult. To address this challenge, we develop GPU-Preprocessor, a GPU-native LP preprocessing framework that integrates folding and presolve. To efficiently implement folding on GPUs, we adapt a randomized partition refinement algorithm to LP folding, using sparse matrix-vector products and parallel sorting to construct stable row and column partitions. For presolve, we introduce a new piecewise-linear reformulation rule that exploits underlying convex piecewise-linear structure to obtain sparser LP representations. We also develop a framework that combines phase scheduling with a Scan-Plan-Apply design to coordinate presolve rules and reduce sparse-matrix reconstruction overhead through batched updates. Numerical experiments on three LP benchmark sets show that GPU-Preprocessor achieves greater average problem-size reductions than PSLP and Gurobi Presolve, with SGM10 preprocessing-time speedups of up to $43.9\times$ and $677.7\times$, respectively. Here, SGM10 denotes the shifted geometric mean with a 10-second shift. On the largest tested quadratic assignment problem LP relaxation, these speedups reach $126.3\times$ and $2{,}207.9\times$. When integrated with the GPU-accelerated LP solver HPR-LP, GPU-Preprocessor achieves SGM10 speedups of $2.5\times$ to $5.0\times$ in combined preprocessing and solving time over HPR-LP without preprocessing. The code is available at https://github.com/PolyU-IOR/GPU-Preprocessor.

title: Safety stock calculation with heteroscedastic, autocorrelated and heavy-tailed forecast errors, an adaptive parametric method.e
abstract: This study develops and validates an adaptive parametric method for sizing safety stock when forecast errors are autocorrelated, heteroscedastic, asymmetric, and heavy-tailed. Using four years of weekly forecasts from a fast-moving consumer goods company, the analysis identifies substantial positive autocorrelation, departures from normality, systematic forecast optimism, and heterogeneous relationships between forecast volume and error variance. The proposed method integrates several corrections into a modular, sequential safety-stock architecture. It constructs cumulative forecast errors over the operational action period, selects an SKU-specific parametric distribution, and determines a baseline protection point using an expected-shortage condition consistent with the target beta fill rate. A forecast-scaled module adjusts dispersion when error variance depends on forecast volume, while a Cycle-End Exposure safeguard limits within-cycle shortage risk when large replenishment lots increase exposure. Performance is evaluated through discrete-event simulation against the company's current method. The proposed method reduces average inventory by 9.9% and maximum inventory by 19.5%, with no statistically significant deterioration in beta fill rate or average stockout duration. The proportion of weeks without stockouts declines slightly, without evidence of more persistent or operationally severe shortages. The heteroscedasticity module provides selective benefits, with greater service improvements as variance dependence intensifies. The resulting framework is interpretable, adapts to SKU-specific statistical profiles, links distributional features to safety-stock outcomes, and can be integrated into existing ERP environments.

title: Online reduced-order modeling from primal solver trajectories for PDE-constrained optimization
abstract: Repeated high-fidelity state and gradient evaluations make large-scale PDE-constrained optimization computationally expensive. Reduced-order modeling provides a natural way to reduce the cost of these repeated high-dimensional computations. However, existing reduced-order modeling approaches often rely on converged high-fidelity states for model construction or updating, while their reduced spaces may lose accuracy as the design moves beyond the region represented by the available data. To address these limitations, we present Reduced-order Trajectory-based Optimization (RETO), an online framework that constructs local reduced-order models (ROMs) directly from unconverged primal solver trajectories. Each local ROM is built from snapshots collected during a finite number of high-fidelity primal iterations, without requiring full-order convergence, and supports multiple low-cost state evaluations, adjoint-based gradient evaluations, and design updates. New solver trajectories are generated at updated design points to reconstruct the local ROM and continue the optimization. Across three distinct PDE-constrained optimization problems, RETO achieves solution quality comparable to that of full-order optimization, with speedups of approximately 8 to 22 times in cases without discontinuities in the state fields. Even in the transonic inverse-design case involving moving shocks, RETO retains an approximately threefold speedup. The transonic results further show that the online local ROM progressively captures evolving shock-related flow features as new primal solver trajectories are incorporated. These results demonstrate the value of unconverged primal solver trajectories as an online information source for reduced-order optimization, allowing the reduced basis to evolve with the design rather than requiring a basis that covers the entire design space in advance.

title: Free-Material Optimization in a Peridynamic World
abstract: We study free-material optimization for nonlinear bond-based nonlocal diffusion and its localization as the interaction horizon $δ$ vanishes. Bond conductivities are subject to pointwise bounds and a global material budget constraint. After normalization, the asymptotic behavior of these problems is governed by the fraction $θ_δ$ of potentially active bonds that can be assigned the maximal conductivity.   We identify three distinct limiting regimes. If $θ_δ\to0$, the normalized optimal values converge to those of the classical vanishing-material optimal design problem, equivalently formulated as a Lipschitz-constrained state problem or a measure-valued flux problem. For $θ_δ\toθ\in(0,1)$, we obtain a directional local free-material problem governed by the upper tail of the directional $p$-strain over position-direction space. Thus the state variable localizes, while the limiting constitutive law retains an internal directional variable inherited from the bonds. If $θ_δ\toθ\geq1$, the limit is the isotropic local $p$-Dirichlet problem.   A convex minimax argument eliminates the normalized conductivity variable exactly, after which the analysis combines convex duality, nonlocal compactness, and $Γ$-convergence for convex integrands. We prove a unified $Γ$-convergence result for the reduced state energies whenever $θ_δ\toθ\in[0,+\infty)$, yielding convergence of normalized optimal values and compactness and identification of optimal states throughout the full parameter range. At the vanishing-material endpoint, we additionally recover optimal measure-valued local fluxes from optimal nonlocal two-point fluxes.

title: On Completely Positive and Semidefinite Programs for Moment Bounds on Maximum of Random Quadratics
abstract: Completely positive programs are known to provide an exact representation to several NP-hard optimization problems. In this work, we look at the maximum of random quadratic functions and compute the maximum expected value over ambiguity sets defined with moment and support information. We propose exact completely positive programs and semidefinite programs when the random variables are Bernoulli, nonnegative and unrestricted in support. Our experimental study demonstrates the utility of these formulations.

title: C1 Virtual Element Methods for the Optimal Control of Oseen Equations with Stream-Function Formulation
abstract: This work analyzes a $C^1$-conforming virtual element method for the optimal control of generalized Oseen equations, formulated using the stream-function on simply connected polygonal domains. The method is based on a conforming discretization in $H^2$ of arbitrary order $k \ge 2$. The discrete scheme considers an approximation of the state and co-state equations which involves a specifically designed operator for the convective term and a \textit{variational discretization} of the control variable. We derive quasi-optimal a priori error estimates in the $H^1$ and $H^2$-norms for the stream-function, and in the $L^2$-norm for the control, under standard assumptions on the family of polygonal meshes. The proposed method recovers the fluid velocity, vorticity, and pressure using suitable projections. Finally, we report several numerical experiments to support the theoretical findings using different polygonal meshes including the cavity problem. We highlight that this analysis also covers OCPs governed by Brinkman and Stokes equation.

title: Time-Inconsistent Singular Dividend Control with Regime Switching and Bankruptcy
abstract: This paper studies infinite-horizon equilibrium dividend distribution for a firm whose surplus follows a diffusion under observable Markov regime switching and is absorbed at bankruptcy. Dividend payments are modeled as singular controls, and non-exponential discounting leads to time inconsistency. We formulate equilibrium control laws and establish a verification theorem for a general finite-state model with surplus-dependent coefficients. For a two-state model with constant positive drifts and volatilities and bi-exponential discounting, we prove the existence of a regime-dependent equilibrium barrier policy for arbitrary positive switching intensities. The policy retains surplus below the prevailing regime's threshold and distributes any excess immediately. Numerical experiments examine how shareholder patience and economic conditions affect dividend decisions. Over the parameter ranges considered, greater discount-rate dispersion at a fixed initial average rate raises both barriers, while switching speed can generate nonmonotone responses and reverse their ordering.

title: The Big Match under translation-invariant charges
abstract: We study two-player zero-sum stochastic games in which a stream of stage payoffs is evaluated by a translation-invariant charge on the set of stages. Every patient valuation, that is, every diffuse charge that obeys the time value of money principle, is translation-invariant, and by Mertens and Neyman each player has, for every $\varepsilon>0$, a strategy that is $\varepsilon$-optimal for all patient valuations simultaneously. We show that this robustness breaks down for translation-invariant charges. In the Big Match with $0$--$1$ payoffs, whose uniform value is $1/2$, every strategy of Player 1 is worthless: for every strategy of Player 1 and every $δ>0$, Player 2 has a pure reply, and there is a translation-invariant charge under which Player 1's payoff is less than $δ$. Consequently, the Big Match has no value with respect to all translation-invariant charges. This contrasts with finite Markov decision processes, where every stationary Blackwell optimal strategy is optimal for every translation-invariant charge. We pose questions on robust guarantees in general stochastic games and on optimality with respect to a fixed translation-invariant charge.

title: Maximizing Reaction via Spatial Localization: A PDE-Constrained Variational Approach
abstract: We study a PDE-constrained variational problem for the optimal spatial distribution of a catalytic material reacting with a substrate in a biological or materials system. With a given catalyst concentration, the substrate concentration is determined by a reaction-diffusion equation. The reaction functional for the catalyst concentrations is defined to be the total reaction output, which is the product of catalyst and substrate concentrations. Both the linear and Michaelis-Menten reaction kinetics are considered. We construct reaction-maximizing sequences through the localization of catalysts using barrier functions and show the non-existence of a global maximizer. We also derive the first and second variations of the reaction functional. By constructing a competing catalyst concentration, we show the non-existence of a local maximizer. Based on our analysis, we propose a regularized variational model and prove the existence of its global maximizer.

title: Convergence Rates of Factorized Gradient Descent for Overparameterized Asymmetric Matrix Sensing with Balancing Regularization
abstract: We study factorized gradient descent (FGD) for overparameterized asymmetric matrix sensing with the balancing regularizer $\frac18\|L^\top L-R^\top R\|_F^2$. An exact indefinite lifting of the population objective decomposes the dynamics of FGD into positive, negative, and null spectral subspaces. The first two components have linear restoring terms, whereas the null component contracts only quadratically. For independent isotropic sub-Gaussian sensing matrices and independent centered sub-Gaussian noise with scale proxy $σ$, we prove the local bound \[   \|L_tR_t^\top-X^\star\|_2   \lesssim\max\left\{\frac{1}{ηt+1/σ_r},   κσ\sqrt{\frac{d_1+d_2}{n}}\right\}, \] under a sufficiently small initialization error, the number of linear measurements $n\gtrsimκ^2(d_1+d_2)\max\{k^2,σ^2/σ_r^2\}$, and step size $η\lesssimσ_1^{-1}$. Here $σ_1$ and $σ_r$ are the largest and smallest nonzero singular values of the target $X^\star\in \mathbb{R}^{d_1\times d_2}$ respectively, and $κ=σ_1/σ_r$. Furthermore, a population trajectory was constructed to have tight product error $Θ(1/t)$. These results provide a local rate characterization for ordinary gradient descent for overparameterized asymmetric matrix sensing with balancing regularizer.

title: Large-Step Last-Iterate Convergence of Random-Reshuffling Stochastic Gradient Descent
abstract: Random reshuffling stochastic gradient descent (RR-SGD) is widely used for finite-sum optimization in machine learning. For convex $L$-smooth components, recent work establishes convergence guarantees for an averaged iterate with component stepsizes as large as order $1/L$. However, the final iterate is a natural output in practice, and existing last-iterate guarantees in this setting require stepsizes that scale inversely with the number of components $n$. We establish an expected objective-gap bound for the last iterate of standard RR-SGD on unconstrained problems with a constant component stepsize satisfying $0<η\lesssim 1/(L(1 + \log(nK)))$, where $K$ is the number of epochs. By retaining the sampling bias at random comparison points, we remove the explicit $1/n$ factor from the stepsize restriction. Combined with existing small-step bounds, our result matches the corresponding averaged-iterate convergence rate up to logarithmic factors.

title: Modeling and Understanding Neural Weights of Humanoid Policies with Diffusion
abstract: Recent advances in robot learning have driven rapid progress in humanoid control, enabling increasingly agile behaviors in the real world. However, humanoid control networks are typically obtained through conventional training procedures, while comparatively little attention has been given to directly modeling the distribution of their learned weights and generating functional networks in weight space. In this work, we investigate whether high-performing humanoid control networks can be generatively modeled directly through their weights. We adopt a latent diffusion framework that couples a linear autoencoder with a Diffusion Transformer. The autoencoder compresses actor network parameters into a compact latent space, and the Diffusion Transformer models the distribution of these latents. Trained on networks collected from reinforcement learning for the Unitree G1 robot, our approach generates deployable networks that perform various motions in the real world, including walking, dancing, and spin kick. Beyond generation, we further study the learned weight space to better understand the structure captured by these humanoid control networks. We identify a structural principle in the first-layer weights that consistently reflects the robot's kinematic prior. Notably, this kinematic prior emerges under both Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Imitation Learning (IL) training, suggesting that it is not specific to a particular optimization process but may instead reflect common knowledge associated with humanoid embodiment. Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of generative modeling in humanoid network weight space, while providing initial insights into the information encoded by their learned weights. Additional results are available on our project website: https://humanoid-weight-diffusion.github.io/

title: Hierarchical Residual Policy Learning for Real-World Mobile Manipulation with Sparse Human Guidance
abstract: Mobile Manipulation (MoMa) is a cornerstone of autonomous robotic systems, yet real-world fine-tuning remains a formidable challenge because of high-dimensional action spaces and intricate coupling between heterogeneous modules. In this paper, we propose HiRe-MoMa (Hierarchical Residual Mobile Manipulation), a systematic framework for stable and sample-efficient real-world fine-tuning of complex MoMa systems. At its core, HiRe-MoMa adopts a Hierarchical Residual Architecture that fine-tunes a frozen base policy. A Policy-Agnostic Residual learns additive corrections atop the base policy, while Hierarchical Decoupling splits the residual into mobile-base and manipulator-arm heads with unidirectional conditioning, mitigating gradient interference and aligning corrections with the platform's physical hierarchy. To improve sample efficiency in data-expensive real-world settings, we propose Expert-Guided Value Alignment, which leverages sparse human interventions with under 20% training coverage to reshape the critic's value landscape, effectively guiding autonomous exploration through expert priors. Extensive real-world experiments on the TIAGo++ platform demonstrate that HiRe-MoMa consistently enhances task performance with only around 30 minutes of online interaction, regardless of the base policy architecture. To our knowledge, this is among the first frameworks to enable efficient on-robot fine-tuning for mobile manipulation in the real world, providing a practical paradigm for deploying complex robotic systems in dynamic, human-centric environments. Further details can be found on our project website: https://hire-moma.github.io/

title: Co-Evolving Acting and Forecasting for Language Agents
abstract:
Training language agents is bottlenecked by the high cost of long-horizon rollouts, yet standard agentic reinforcement learning (RL) learns only from a terminal scalar reward, leaving the supervision in intermediate steps largely unused. Prior work exploits this supervision through value targets that estimate per-step success probabilities or observation targets that fit environment response. Both are hard to construct well: (1) value targets come from the same single scalar signal for each step in the trajectory, and (2) observation targets, such as web pages and terminal logs, are long and noisy and reach only one step ahead. We propose 
ame, which adds a third kind of multi-step action targets. On successful on-policy trajectories, 
ame trains the policy backbone to generate the action sequences that follows each history. Each action is also supervised when forecast from the preceding histories, forming a temporal ensemble that the shared backbone absorbs during training, and this enables acting and forecasting to co-evolve. The policy still acts one step at a time at inference, with no overhead. Across five benchmarks (ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, WebShop, $τ^2$-bench, and AppWorld), 
ame (1) achieves stronger aggregate performance than GRPO and RL baselines with predictive auxiliary targets across simulated environments, while improving overall performance on both realistic applications; (2) delivers up to $1.9	imes$ and $2.0	imes$ higher sample efficiency than ECHO and GRPO, respectively, on ScienceWorld; and (3) achieves these gains with a single policy backbone, without additional models, separate pretraining, or inference overhead. The codebase is available at https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/CoPE.

title: Your Transformer Is Secretly Elastic
abstract: Scaling up transformers has produced models with broad capabilities, deployed across heterogeneous hardware and fluctuating workloads. Yet, model families offer only a few fixed sizes (e.g., S, B, L), forcing users to commit to a model based on hardware and latency constraints. This rigidity is often suboptimal under varying query loads. We introduce a retraining-free method that elastifies pre-trained transformers into a single model that adapts on-the-fly across a continuum of computational budgets. Our key contribution is a differentiable relaxation of the functional unit-ranking problem: unlike prior work, which optimizes a single importance weight per MLP block or attention head, we rank every individual MLP neuron and attention head jointly, on a common scale, by minimizing the model's loss under soft pruning across many sparsity targets, all at once.
