abstract: Image-token compression must reduce computation without hurting the semantics. We introduce Varest, guided by semantic fungibility: tokens within a coherent semantic region can be summarized coarsely, while object boundaries and literal text require finer distinctions. Object and text localizers guide variable-resolution merging, preserving spatial coverage and finer detail at boundaries and text. Learned [REL] registers then prune visual tokens after early decoder processing. Training across budgets enables one checkpoint per backbone. Across three backbones and 13 benchmarks, Varest outperforms 15 baselines in mean performance retention at every evaluated budget, retaining 86.10-92.33% of full-token performance with only 5.56% of the original layer-averaged image-token count.

title: RadarGSOcc: Doppler-Aware 3D Semantic Occupancy Prediction Using 4D Radar Tensor with Geometric-Semantic Feature Extraction
abstract: 3D semantic occupancy prediction is crucial for autonomous driving, but camera-based methods degrade in low-light conditions and LiDAR-based methods are sensitive to adverse weather. 4D radar is more robust, yet its sparsity and the high cost of radar tensor processing limit its use. We propose Radar Geometric-Semantic Occupancy Prediction (RadarGSOcc), an efficient framework that directly processes 4D radar tensors by separately extracting geometric and semantic features, including Doppler information, with a deformable attention-based geometric refinement module as its key component. We also introduce the K-Radar 3DSemOcc benchmark, the first large-scale benchmark for 3D semantic occupancy prediction using 4D radar tensors, built on the K-Radar dataset with refined LiDAR-based annotations. RadarGSOcc predicts 15 classes within a 51.2m range and achieves 38.2% IoU, 7.6% mIoU, and 25.5% weighted mIoU, outperforming RadarOcc by 17% relative (25.5 vs. 21.9) in weighted mIoU while using fewer parameters and lower computation. It substantially improves truck prediction while trading off car accuracy, outperforms camera-based approaches, and narrows the gap with LiDAR-based methods. To assess robustness without per-frame ground truth in adverse weather, we further propose a novel proxy metric, Environment-Based KL Divergence (EBKL), under which 4D radar proves a reliable and efficient modality for 3D semantic occupancy prediction. The dataset and code will be publicly available.

title: Knowing the User Is Not Knowing What We Established: Grounding Awareness in Personal Agents
abstract: Personal-agent memory has largely focused on learning what users know, prefer, and want. However, knowing the user does not necessarily mean knowing what the user and the agent have established together. An assistant's proposal should not become an authorized instruction merely because it is remembered. We introduce Grounding Awareness, the ability to distinguish accepted, unacknowledged, revised, and scoped arrangements when selecting actions. We develop a controlled benchmark to test whether agents can tell the difference between proposals users have accepted and those they have not, and whether they apply accepted arrangements only where appropriate. Across multiple agents and memory systems, we find that strong memory performance does not ensure Grounding Awareness. More surprisingly, providing more complete user information can increase execution of unacknowledged proposals, while persistent memory can cause agents to treat these proposals as if they were user instructions. We trace these failures through memory writing, retrieval, and action selection. Finally, we introduce Grounding Layer, a lightweight, training-free extension that explicitly tracks grounding status and checks consequential actions, substantially improving agent behavior without modifying models or memory systems.

title: ProAS: A Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping Framework for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as the primary paradigm for optimizing Large Language Model (LLM) agents, yet efficient critic-free algorithms (e.g., GRPO) suffer from a fundamental uniform credit assignment dilemma that broadcasts trajectory-level advantages equally to all actions. Our analysis reveals that this uniformity inherently reinforces structurally invalid actions in preferred trajectories and ignores the downstream cascading influence of early pivotal deviations in unpreferred ones. To resolve this without introducing critic overhead, we propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), a plug-and-play framework that leverages a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG) to achieve fine-grained credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR). Extensive experiments across Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct demonstrate that ProAS universally elevates mainstream group-based baselines to new state-of-the-art performance, achieving peak success rates of 91.9\% and 94.3\% on ALFWorld, alongside 66.7\% and 70.8\% on WebShop, respectively. Furthermore, it accelerates training convergence by up to $2.44\times$ while maintaining strong robustness against imperfect or distilled ARGs. Codes: https://github.com/LINs-lab/ProAS.

title: Model-Based Online Decision Making via Generative Trajectory Planning
abstract: Online decision-making faces a tension between efficient inference and long-horizon reasoning. Value-based methods rely on short-horizon bootstrapping that limits the propagation of long-term information, while trajectory optimization methods plan explicitly but must solve a high-dimensional optimization problem at every decision step. We propose Generative Trajectory Planning (GTP), a model-based framework that addresses this tension by learning a generative model as a proposal distribution over action sequences. Instead of optimizing sequences from scratch, GTP samples candidate sequences from a diffusion prior and refines them using learned dynamics, reward, and value models, enabling efficient trajectory-level reasoning. Across continuous control and long-horizon manipulation tasks, GTP matches or exceeds state-of-the-art model-free, diffusion-policy, and model-based baselines, and remains stable in regimes where strong baselines degrade. Our results suggest that generative models are best understood not as policies, but as structured proposal distributions for planning, offering a new perspective on how to integrate generative modeling with model-based decision-making.

title: From Relation-Specific Heads to Shared Interventions: Contextual Entrainment in Language Models
abstract: Large language models rely on prompt context to perform in-context learning, follow formats, and adapt to local evidence. This ability, however, also raises a robustness concern: models may reuse irrelevant tokens from earlier context when answering a later query. Prior work identifies this behavior as contextual entrainment and finds attention heads whose ablation reduces it, arguing that these heads are largely task- or relation-specific. But are the mechanisms behind contextual entrainment truly isolated by relation, or do relation-conditioned searches recover reusable components shared across relations? Using factual-distractor relation-completion prompts across 19 lexical-semantic subtypes, we identify attention heads whose ablation reduces entrainment and test how the resulting head sets transfer recovery ability across exact relations, semantic families, and mixed relation distributions. Same-family transfer exceeds different-family transfer, family residuals weaken once globally shared heads are removed, and subtype-specific searches repeatedly rediscover many global heads. Clean-completion and context-use probes further suggest that this shared intervention can reduce harmful copying while preserving ordinary relation completion and simple in-context abilities. Our findings provide a more precise perspective on contextual entrainment and its mitigation: harmful context following is not best addressed by searching for isolated relation-specific circuits, but by using heterogeneous attack prompts to reveal reusable intervention targets whose effects are shaped by semantic relation structure.

title: SMI: Ontology-Grounded Semantic IDs for Hierarchy-Aware Medical Concept Representation
abstract: Biomedical language models (LMs) provide strong representations for clinical tasks, but they often fail to capture the hierarchical structure among medical concepts. This limitation is especially pronounced for rare and fine-grained clinical codes in long-tailed vocabularies, where hierarchy-agnostic LM representations become less informative as concept frequency decreases. We introduce Semantic Medical Identifier (SMI), a training-free framework for constructing ontology-grounded Semantic IDs and hierarchy-aware medical concept representations. For each diagnosis, procedure, or medication concept, SMI defines its Semantic ID as the coarse-to-fine path through an expert-defined medical ontology. SMI then aggregates frozen biomedical LM embeddings across the corresponding ontology levels to form hierarchy-aware medical concept representations that preserve coarse-to-fine clinical semantics. The base SMI uses uniform aggregation across ontology levels, while a level-weighted variant selects global level weights on validation data. Our theoretical analysis shows that SMI yields more informative medical concept representations than hierarchy-agnostic LM embeddings, particularly for rare and fine-grained clinical concepts. Experiments show that SMI captures meaningful hierarchical structure and improves clinical relation prediction. On MIMIC-IV, SMI improves mortality prediction, readmission prediction, drug recommendation, and rare drug prediction. On eICU, SMI yields more robust patient representations under cross-hospital distribution shift.

title: Known-Voice Cloning and the Limits of Personality Transfer for Character Design
abstract: Recent advances in zero-shot voice cloning systems make it possible to reproduce a recognizable voice from a short recording and attach it to arbitrary virtual characters. Prior work suggests that familiar vocal identity can carry over associated personality impressions to new targets such as robots or virtual characters. However, these works have mainly examined familiarity and personalization effects rather than directly testing whether a cloned familiar voice systematically transfers personality impressions to an embodied virtual character. Such transference raises the concern that cloned voices could be used to manipulate people into engaging with virtual characters as capable social actors. Across two studies, we investigated whether personality impressions transfer when a virtual character speaks with the cloned voice of a familiar person. Study 1 examined this question in a real-world university setting using the cloned voice of a lecturer familiar to the participating students. Study 2 examined the same question online using voices of social media content creators and members of their communities. Drawing on the concepts of identity activation, trait transfer, and person reconstruction, we show that evidence of personality transfer was limited in both studies. Observed effects were selective and did not generalize across traits or study contexts. In the online study in particular, recognizable voice identity cues activated expectations about the speaker but did not reconstruct the broader person impression. Qualitative responses further indicated that judgments were frequently shaped by perceived artificiality and by whether voice and appearance fit together. Our findings moderate common concerns that cloned voices straightforwardly manipulate people into perceiving artificial characters as capable social actors.

title: Kwai Summary Attention V2 Technical Report
abstract: Summary-token architectures such as Kwai Summary Attention (KSA) compress distant context into learnable Summary token per chunk, and hybrid variants interleave these layers with full attention to retain exact access to the original text. In such hybrid KSA-Full architecture, the interleaving inserted summary tokens are served as a streaming flow role across different layers. Although effective, however, it also introduce some bottlenecks: (1) the different layers summary compression chunk must be same, therefore hard to reach a flexible KV Cache compression, e.g., different layer set different summary compression chunk window. (2) in the full-attention layers, the summary token introduced additional computation cost, but such layer ignore them and still pay quadratic prefilling, therefore unfriendly to the computation side. Motivated by them, we developed the KSA V2, which not only achieves a more flexible KV cache memory compression but also reduces the computation cost in Full attention layer. Specifically, we found that the summary tokens can serve two roles: the KV memory and sparse indexer.

title: AMemOps: Evaluating Memory Updates in Long Audio Streams
abstract: Audio memory must recognise recurring sources across acoustic changes while keeping their attributes up to date. Overall accuracy does not reveal how these demands interact. We introduce Audio Memory Operations (AMemOps), a benchmark for latest-attribute retrieval, preservation of unchanged attributes and absent-source rejection in long audio streams. Paired controls vary recordings, training identities and earlier events to examine their effects on updating. Training on other recordings of the test instruments increases a reference delta-rule memory's update advantage over matched attention by 13.4 percentage points. At retrieval delays of 120\,s, matched histories separate benefits of consistent repetition from costs of conflicting earlier values, while additive-memory controls identify benefits of erasure.

title: Tiny Recursive Message Passing
abstract: Message passing neural networks have shown remarkable performance in algorithmic and constraint reasoning, due to their ability to encode the structure of the task directly in the architecture. Recent work has shown that better results can be achieved using recursive transformers trained with deep supervision and truncated recursions, which make extremely deep loops stable to train, and equipped with test-time procedures such as discrete deduction lattices. In this work, we apply the same procedures to message passing networks, and show that the two ingredients are complementary, and lead to parameter efficient models: we obtain about $99\%$ test accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme with a model of $16$k parameters that trains in about $10$ minutes on an H100, or in $9$ hours on a CPU. We further show that the cost of truncating gradients grows with the number of rounds information needs to cross the graph, making the choice of wiring a trade-off between robustness to truncation and transfer across problem sizes. We conclude by showing that our models transfer zero-shot to larger instances than those seen during training, outperforming popular neural baselines on N-queens and Boolean satisfiability with a fraction of their parameters.

title: ST-GRU PredRNN-V2: A GRU-Based Reformulation of PredRNN-V2 for Video Prediction
abstract: Video prediction requires models to capture complex spatiotemporal dependencies and to retain relevant information over long sequences. PredRNN and its successor PredRNN-V2 address this challenge with spatiotemporal Long Short-Term Memory (ST-LSTM) units that maintain two separate memory states, at the cost of a relatively complex recurrent building block. In this work, we investigate whether the simpler gating of Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) can be transferred to spatiotemporal predictive learning. To this end, we develop a spatiotemporal GRU (ST-GRU) unit as a GRU-based alternative to the ST-LSTM. The ST-GRU replaces the ST-LSTM's three gates per memory state with two GRU-style gates (update and reset), and merges the temporal memory state into the hidden state, which reduces the number of parameters by about 5%. We incorporate the ST-GRU into PredRNN-V2 and evaluate the resulting model on the Moving MNIST video prediction benchmark, following the original experimental protocol. Averaged over ten predicted frames, the ST-GRU-based PredRNN-V2 achieves an MSE of 55.1, an SSIM of 0.883, an LPIPS of 0.065 and a PSNR of 19.53dB. It does not surpass the original ST-LSTM-based PredRNN-V2 on MSE, SSIM or PSNR, but it achieves a lower LPIPS and performs on par with the earlier ST-LSTM-based PredRNN, while using a simpler recurrent cell. These results suggest that ST-GRUs are a promising building block for spatiotemporal predictive learning and motivate further work on their design and integration.

title: To Align or Not To Align: Check Your COMPASS Before You Train
abstract: Combining pretrained models is a common strategy for building AI systems, whether by aligning a vision encoder with a language model or merging fine-tuned checkpoints. However, finding compatible pairs typically requires costly empirical search, as compatibility is known only after alignment or merging. We propose COMPASS (COMPatibility ASsessment Score), a theoretically motivated diagnostic that estimates whether a model pair will be compatible prior to alignment or merging. Building on the observation that representational convergence is most robust at the level of local neighborhoods, COMPASS decomposes model compatibility into two cheap-to-compute axes: a pair-specific ease, defined as the $k$-NN overlap between the two encoders, and a paradigm-level ceiling, capturing the maximum overlap their training paradigms allow. Together, these two axes provide a ranking of candidate model pairs and prescribe how to act on each pair: (i) prioritize pairs that already agree and whose paradigms are compatible, (ii) invest additional compute on pairs with compatible paradigms but low initial agreement, (iii) switch the pretraining paradigm when it cannot support sufficient agreement, or (iv) deprioritize pairs that score poorly on both axes. We apply COMPASS to $72$ cross-modal alignment experiments and $392$ task-arithmetic model merges and show that compatibility estimates by COMPASS strongly correlate with downstream success, achieving average Pearson correlation of $0.91$ on cross-modal alignment tasks and $0.70$ on model merging.

title: DTScribe: Generating Models for Digital Twin Reporting using Local Large Language Models
abstract: The development of a digital twin brings together many stakeholders and technical components. We have previously investigated the reporting of the conceptual architecture for these digital twins as an artifact for discussion. However, we find that the activity of modeling the digital twin for visualization and consensus-building can be quite tedious and time-consuming.   In this article, we explore the automation of model generation using large language models, targeting the model required for digital twin reporting. Our approach is designed to ingest digital twin documents and output both the conceptual architecture visualization and a reporting page for that digital twin. We first extract from the input the key details aligning with our twenty-one-characteristic Digital Twin Description Framework described in previous work. Then, we generate a description model in the Ontological Modeling Language, representing the digital twin as a constellation of models, data, enablers, and services. We utilize refinement loops with large language models acting as judges and ontological reasoning to increase artifact quality as measured by our metrics.   We investigate how architectural and parameter choices affect artifact quality, such as how refinement loops enable local large language models to produce sufficiently high-quality results comparable to larger models. We also detail insights and lessons learned useful for practitioners, such that they can integrate our techniques to accelerate their digital twin reporting or for other model generation tasks. These insights include the use of medium-sized local models (around 20 billion parameters), the avoidance of large language models as judges and clustering for characteristic extraction, and the recommendation of at least two reasoner loops for Ontological Modeling Language refinement.

title: Geometric Calibration of Supervised Fine-Tuning
abstract: Recent studies investigate the weight geometry through its spectral structure, which characterizes how the weights transform different input directions. Within this view, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is shown to induce dense updates that perturb the spectral geometry of pre-SFT weights along their principal directions, potentially disrupting the model's prior knowledge. These observations motivate using the geometry of pre-SFT weights as a reference for refining learned SFT updates. We study this perspective as Geometric Calibration and develop SPACE Subspace Projection for Adapted Checkpoint Enhancement), a lightweight post-hoc method that selectively reverts SFT update components within the principal subspace of the pre-SFT weights while preserving those in its orthogonal complement. SPACE is a data-free, training-free method that requires only the pre- and post-SFT checkpoints. We evaluate SPACE on Qwen2.5, Qwen3, Qwen3.5, Llama-3.1, and Olmo-3 models ranging from 2B to 14B, across mathematical, coding, and medical SFT, as well as several SFT variants. Overall, SPACE mitigates out-of-domain (OOD) capability regression while further improving in-domain (ID) performance over the uncalibrated SFT checkpoints. For math SFT, SPACE yields average ID/OOD gains of 2.85/2.26 points on Qwen2.5-7B, and 2.41/1.52 points on Qwen3-14B-Base, respectively. These results highlight how the geometric relationship between SFT updates and pre-SFT weights shapes the adapted model's capabilities and, more broadly, motivate geometry-aware parameter updates for continual model improvement.

title: Falsification-proof non-market allocation mechanisms
abstract: Relying on manipulable characteristics to target the allocation of resources is fraught with difficulties. Naively optimal rules lead to falsification and allocative inefficiency. Optimizing the rule for allocative efficiency while accounting for falsification typically induces falsification, at a heavy cost to the agents. Moreover, falsification generates negative externalities. We characterize optimal falsification-proof rules under a broad range of falsification technologies. We also provide an honesty condition under which they solve the unconstrained problem of a planner who maximizes a weighted sum of allocative surplus and agents' welfare.

title: Two Routes to Interoceptive Prioritisation: Dissociating Likelihood Precision and Preference Reweighting in Active Inference
abstract: An embodied agent must prioritise among competing bodily needs. In active inference, it can respond to an urgent need by increasing the precision of information about that need or by increasing its preference for outcomes that relieve it. We compare these two interventions, separately and together, in a foraging gridworld with three lethal needs, and ask how each changes survival, perception and the body model the agent learns. Precision sharpens interoceptive posteriors and improves survival. Preference reweighting keeps bodily states further from their lethal boundaries and changes the states from which the agent learns, so its learned model covers fewer need levels, with lower quality across all levels but slightly higher quality on the levels it visits. An experiment on 72 further layouts does not establish the predicted preference benefit on difficult layouts, but both interventions improve average survival there and their interaction is positive. Survival alone therefore gives an incomplete account of how a model prioritises needs and learns about its body.

title: Knowledge Graphs as Files: An Agent Harness Where Tool Creation and Tool Use Co-Evolve
abstract: Searching text-rich knowledge graphs requires following relations while examining textual evidence. Predefined graph interfaces constrain what evidence agents can access, even when they write code to combine tool calls or process retrieved subgraphs. We propose direct knowledge graph interaction (DKGI), a harness in which language model agents create graph access tools directly over complete node and edge files. The agent writes Python code to follow relations, combine node sets, and select textual evidence, interleaving execution with shell search and file inspection. This lets agents process large node sets in bulk while returning selected text for the model to assess. Execution feedback guides tool creation and revision, while the evolving tools determine what evidence the agent gathers next. On benchmark datasets spanning three domains, training-free DKGI exceeds the strongest published baseline by at least 6.7 Hit@1 points on every graph, even with a minimal harness. Controlled ablations show the benefits of multi-turn programming over shell-only access and predefined graph tools, while trajectories show agents revising code to extend searches or address errors. These findings highlight the value of allowing tool creation and tool use to co-evolve during graph search. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/leopoldwhite/DKGI.

title: Can an Agent Learn to Predict Its Own Failure? Outcome-Grounded Confidence Calibration in LLM Agents
abstract: Controlling an acting LLM agent means deciding, at each step of a long-horizon task, whether to trust its next action, abstain, or hand off to a human. That decision needs a per-step confidence signal predicting whether the current rollout will eventually succeed. The agent's own self-reported verbalized confidence is the natural candidate, but existing reinforcement learning methods calibrate it against the correctness of a decision at the current step. We propose a method to calibrate it against the eventual outcome of a multi-step episode: under GRPO, the group of rollouts for a task supplies success labels, and a proper scoring rule scores each step's confidence against the realized outcome. In offline RL on recorded trajectories of a Qwen2.5-7B agent in ALFWorld, TextWorld, and WebShop environments, the AUROC of step confidence against episode outcome rises from near chance to 0.68-0.85, and the top-10% of steps the agent is most confident about succeed ~4.3x more often than average. In online RL on the live ALFWorld agent, four calibration rewards improve early-step AUROC, expected calibration error goes from 0.42 to below 0.12, and selective execution improves over both the untrained agent and a format-only RL control, without degrading task success. We also introduce an evaluation protocol that separates episode depth, task difficulty, and attempt-level foresight, which shows where the gain lies: the trained agent recognizes from its first step which tasks it will fail, while telling a succeeding attempt from a failing one at the same task is harder, with some early-window signal emerging on TextWorld.

title: Does self-distillation improve reasoning?
abstract: Self-distillation is an emerging approach that trains a model to imitate its own predictions when conditioned on privileged information, such as correct answers or environmental feedback. Recent methods have reported better sample efficiency and generalization than reinforcement learning (RL), but it remains unclear whether these gains extend beyond in-distribution evaluations and whether they stem from privileged distillation. In this paper, we revisit two representative methods, Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) and On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), across code, science, tool use, and math reasoning tasks. We find that their reported gains do not consistently generalize to unseen problems and are largely explained by overfitting or transferring existing reasoning behavior, rather than effectively using privileged information. Moreover, self-distillation gradients show weak alignment with policy gradients that directly optimize expected reward, questioning whether they provide an effective direction for policy improvement. Our experiments across Qwen3 models (1.7B-14B) and OLMo-3-7B suggest that effectively leveraging privileged information to improve reasoning remains an open challenge. Our code is available at https://github.com/sleepypandu/does-sd-improve-reasoning

title: Settling the Approximability of Submodular Facility Location
abstract: In submodular facility location (SFL), introduced by Svitkina and Tardos (SODA 2006), clients $\cal C$ in a metric space are assigned to facilities $\cal F$. A facility serving a set $S \subseteq \cal C$ of clients incurs cost $g(S)$, where $g$ is a monotone submodular function common to all facilities. The best known approximation factor for SFL is $O(\log\log|\cal C|)$, due to Abbasi, Adamczyk, Bosch-Calvo, Byrka, Grandoni, Sornat, and Tinguely (ICALP 2024), improving on the $O(\log|\cal C|)$-approximation of Svitkina and Tardos. We show that this is best possible up to a constant factor in the value-oracle model by showing that there exists no algorithm with only polynomially many queries to $g$ with approximation ratio $o(\log\log|\cal C|)$. This bound holds for algorithms with unlimited computation time, and when $g$ is restricted to matroid rank functions. We also show that the natural linear programming relaxation has an integrality gap of $Θ(\log\log|\cal C|)$. Our lower bound follows by constructing an extension of Vondrák's symmetry-gap approach (FOCS 2009) for matroid rank functions.

title: Bipartite Matching with Few Rounds of Demand Queries
abstract: We study the randomised and deterministic demand-query complexity of approximate bipartite matching with few query rounds. The demand-query model, introduced in [Blumrosen and Nisan SICOMP 2009; Nisan SODA 2021], is inspired by combinatorial auctions and welfare maximisation, where an oracle returns the first neighbouring vertex (item) of a vertex u (agent) according to a given permutation pi (preference ordering of the agent over the items).   For randomised algorithms, our main result gives a trade-off between the number of rounds k, the per-round query budget q=n^{1+δ}, and the achievable approximation ratio. Let 1 <= k <= log n, and -1 <= delta <= 1/k. Every k-round randomised algorithm using O(q) demand queries per round has a worst-case expected-size approximation factor of Omega(n^{1/2k-delta/2}/k). Conversely, we give a randomised algorithm achieving approximation factor O(n^{(1-k*delta)/(k+1)}/k) in expectation.   For deterministic algorithms, for k*q >= n, we show that the optimal deterministic approximation factor is ~Theta(n^2/(q*k^2)), thereby improving the previous lower bound of [Nisan SODA 2021] by a polynomial factor over a wide range of parameters. In particular, for q=Theta(n), we improve the deterministic round-complexity lower bound for constant-factor approximation from ~Omega(n^{1/3}) to ~Omega(sqrt n). Our algorithms produce matching and vertex-cover certificates; the deterministic trade-off also extends to minimum vertex cover and maximum fractional matching.   We extend the randomised upper bounds to the weaker Demand-OR model [Nisan 2021]. We prove a non-adaptive simulation of uniform random-neighbour queries using known techniques, avoiding the O(log n)-round penalty of the trivial binary-search simulation. Consequently, our upper bounds yield the same k-round approximation guarantees using O(q * log^2 n) Demand-OR queries per round.

title: Two Holes Make a Difference: Deterministic Paging with Delay and Deadlines
abstract: In this paper, we study online paging with delay or deadlines. In online paging with delay, an online algorithm manages a cache of size $k$ and needs to serve incoming requests by adding the requested pages to the cache. In addition, it has the option to delay serving incoming requests at a cost that depends on the delay. We propose a new online algorithm, which combines a threshold rule with first-in, first-out (FIFO) replacement, and show that it is $(2k+2)$-competitive for cache size $k$. This result corrects a previously published claim that the competitive ratio is exactly $2k+1$ regardless of the number of holes (pages outside the cache). However, in the case of one hole, we show that the FIFO rule with a different threshold is indeed $(2k+1)$-competitive, giving a tight result.   In the case of deadlines, the same analysis gives a deadline-triggered algorithm that is $(k+1)$-competitive in general and $k$-competitive if there is only one hole. Moreover, we show that the second hole makes paging with deadlines strictly harder than classical paging, where the competitive ratio is independent of the number of holes. For paging with deadlines, we prove a deterministic lower bound of $k+\tfrac12$, already for two holes. We show that, as a consequence, no threshold-triggered algorithm can achieve a competitive ratio less than $2k+\frac32$ in general.

title: Selecting the 7th Smallest of 16 Elements Takes Exactly 28 Comparisons
abstract: Let $V_i(n)$ denote the minimum worst-case number of comparisons needed to find the $i$-th smallest of $n$ distinct elements. We construct algorithms showing $V_7(16)\le28$ and $V_8(16)\le29$, improving the previously reported upper bounds of 30 and 31. Together with known lower bounds, these results establish $V_7(16)=28$ and leave $V_8(16)\in\{28,29\}$. For 17 elements, we establish $V_5(17)=27$ and improve the upper bounds for ranks 6 through 9 to 29, 30, 31, and 31, respectively. Every new upper bound has an explicit decision-graph certificate verified by a static checker developed independently of the search. We also derive a lower bound for selection from a partially ordered state by combining the Fussenegger-Gabow weight with its order-reversed counterpart. All new upper bounds and this lower bound are formally verified in Lean 4. For $V_8(16)$, we show that a lower bound based solely on the total number of decision-tree leaves cannot establish $V_8(16)\ge29$. The algorithms were found using fixed-budget search, information-guided comparison ordering, and proof-number search. Proof-number search was decisive in finding the 28-comparison algorithm; in our experiments, refuting a comparison budget remained substantially more expensive than finding an algorithm within it.

title: Optimal Support Size Testing
abstract: We present an optimal tester for support size that determines whether an unknown probability distribution is supported on $n$ elements or $\varepsilon$-far away (in total variation distance) with sample complexity $Θ(\frac{n}{\varepsilon\log(n)})$, improving the prior best $O(\frac{n}{\varepsilon\log(n)} \log(\min\{\frac{1}{\varepsilon}, n\}))$ due to Ferreira Pinto Jr. and Harms (STOC 2025). As a generalization, we provide a pretty good lower bound on support size.

title: Exploring Minimal Blocking Sets for Kernelization Lower Bounds for $\mathcal{F}$-Minor Deletion
abstract: For Vertex Cover, a minimal blocking set of a graph $G$ is an inclusion-wise minimal vertex set contained in no minimum vertex cover of $G$. Bougeret et al. [SIDMA 2022] showed that, for all minor-closed graph classes $\mathcal{G}$, Vertex Cover has a polynomial kernel parameterized by the distance to $\mathcal{G}$ if and only if $\mathcal{G}$ has bounded minimal blocking sets.   In this work, we explore how far this connection between minimal blocking sets and kernelization extends to $\mathcal{F}$-Minor Deletion parameterized by the deletion distance to $\mathcal{G}$. A minimal $\mathcal{F}$-blocking set of $G$ is a minimal vertex set not contained in any optimal $\mathcal{F}$-Minor Deletion solution of $G$. For connected families $\mathcal{F}$, we show that if some graph class $\mathcal{G}$ closed under disjoint union has unbounded minimal $\mathcal{F}$-blocking sets, then $\mathcal{F}$-Minor Deletion parameterized by the deletion distance to $\mathcal{G}$ has no polynomial kernel. This generalizes a result of Hols et al. [SIDMA 2022] for Vertex Cover. We then show that this criterion does not capture all kernelization lower bounds for $\mathcal{F}$-Minor Deletion, even for minor-closed graph classes. Motivated by the work of Dekker and Jansen [Discrete Appl. Math. 2024], we study the more general notion of extended $\mathcal{F}$-blocking sets and the kernelization lower bounds they yield.   For every fixed integer $η\geq 1$, Pw-$η$ Deletion is the problem of deleting at most $k$ vertices to reduce the pathwidth to at most $η$. We show that it has no polynomial kernel parameterized by the distance to graphs with pathwidth at most $η+1$. Moreover, for connected families $\mathcal{F}$, we show that $\mathcal{F}$-Minor Deletion parameterized by the distance to graphs with pathwidth at most $\max_{F\in\mathcal{F}} pw(F)+1$ has no polynomial kernel.

title: Semi-Streaming Estimation of the Held--Karp Bound and Graph-Metric TSP Cost
abstract: The Held--Karp bound is a linear-programming lower bound for the metric traveling salesperson problem (TSP). We approximate this bound in the multi-pass insertion-only streaming model for metrics induced by connected positive-weight graphs. For an $n$-vertex, $m$-edge graph and $0<\eps\le1/2$, the algorithm returns a $(1+\eps)$ upper approximation with high probability, using $\wtO(\eps^{-4})$ passes, $\wtO(n\eps^{-2})$ words, and $\wtO(m\eps^{-4})$ arithmetic operations per pass.   We replace the changing edge-weight vector by a short history of multiplicative-weights (MWU) updates. After initialization, updates repeat until a column is removed. We store each repeated update once, with its repetition count. The record length depends on the number of columns, not updates; the argument applies to any fixed nonnegative matrix. For Held--Karp, tree-path queries recover edge weights from these records. Separate search and update thresholds allow fresh sparsifiers at successive search stages. Controlled rounding gives a bounded-precision implementation.   The estimate yields a $(3/2+\eps)$ graph-metric TSP value estimate and a $(7/5+\eps)$ estimate when the input graph is unweighted. Conversely, in weighted graph streams, every one-pass $(1+η)$ upper approximation to Held--Karp, for fixed $0\leη<1$, requires quadratic space. The algorithms estimate values; they do not construct tours within these bounds.

title: Sublinear-Time and Semi-Streaming Algorithms for Path Cover and TSP
abstract: We give improved sublinear-time and semi-streaming approximation algorithms for maximum path cover, $(1,2)$-TSP, and Max-TSP. For each fixed $\eps>0$, our distance-query algorithm estimates the optimum cost of an $n$-vertex $(1,2)$-TSP instance from above within factor $2-\cstar+\eps=1.413184\ldots+\eps$, with high probability, in $n^{2-Ω_\eps(1)}$ time, where $\cstar=2(\sec1-\tan1)$. This improves the $3/2+\eps$ factor of direct matching estimation in this subquadratic regime~\cite{BhattacharyaKissSaranurak2023} and of the faster near-linear estimator~\cite{BehnezhadEtAl2024}. A single random vertex order defines an implicit bipartite graph whose matchings project to path covers. An alternating-permutation analysis shows that its expected maximum matching size is at least $\cstar$ times the optimum path-cover size. On long paths, even the best of polynomially many uniform orders retains only a $\cstar+o(1)$ fraction with high probability.   In semi-streaming, we construct deterministic $(5/7-\eps)$-approximate unweighted path covers and $(9/7+\eps+5/(7n))$-approximate $(1,2)$-TSP tours, improving the respective $2/3-\eps$ and $4/3+\eps+1/n$ guarantees in~\cite{AlipourFarokhnejadMoemke2025}. For nonnegative weights, we obtain $2/3-\eps$ for path cover and Max-TSP, improving the earlier asymptotic $7/12-\eps$ Max-TSP bound. These algorithms use $\poly(1/\eps)$ passes independent of $n$ and $O(n\log(n/\eps)\poly(1/\eps))$ words. We compute two approximate matchings separated by edge deletion. A cycle-compensation lemma accounts for the weight removed when breaking their cycles. For unweighted graphs, a third approximate matching on a simple auxiliary graph with at most $2n$ vertices chooses component connections; a Tutte--Berge count proves the stronger bound.

title: A Randomized Approximation Algorithm for Doubly Free-Boundary Macdonald Processes
abstract: We construct an approximate sampler for finite doubly free-boundary Macdonald rail-yard processes with Macdonald, boundary, and edge parameters in $(0,1)$. The construction allows arbitrary finite sequences of additions and removals of horizontal or vertical strips and all four boundary types. It reverses a finite commutation--reflection history from a partition sequence whose entries are equal, with the common partition weighted by both boundaries. We derive local reconstruction kernels from the skew Cauchy, Littlewood, and branching identities. Bulk and boundary updates combine integer increments with conditional shape sampling at a prescribed size; same-sign swaps use finite conditional resampling.   For $K$ reflection periods and an initial partition-size cutoff $M$, the algorithm terminates almost surely and samples the resulting approximating law exactly. We prove total variation convergence to the target process as $K,M\to\infty$ and give explicit bounds for both truncation errors, decaying geometrically in the cutoffs for fixed input parameters. Under fixed parameter bounds, we also bound the expected operation count of direct enumeration in a unit-cost model.   We further construct an exact rejection sampler for the initial partition law without a size cutoff or evaluation of its normalizing constant. Using this sampler removes the size-truncation error, leaving only the error from the finite reflection history.

title: Subgaussian Vector Balancing by an Ising Model
abstract: We show that the guaranties of the Gram-Schmidt Walk Algorithm of Bansal, Dadush, Garg, and Lovett can be achieved by an Ising model. Given vectors $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ of norm less than 1, we give a closed form for a centrally symmetric distribution on a vector $σ\in \{\pm 1 \}^n$ so that the signed sum $\sum_j σ(j) v_j$ is $1$-subgaussian. We show that the Glauber dynamics for this model mix rapidly provided that the norms of the input vectors are bounded below 1 by an inverse-polynomial.   The proofs employ the theory of Lorentzian polynomials, and we use these techniques to show fast mixing bounds for other spin systems.

title: Solving SAT via Treewidth Backdoors in Linear Time: Beyond Sparsity
abstract: The Boolean Satisfiability (SAT) problem is a remarkably expressive computational problem, serving both as a cornerstone of complexity theory and as a unifying language for a wide range of search and reasoning tasks. While $\mathrm{NP}$-complete in general, SAT is well known to be linear-time solvable on instances with bounded treewidth. This motivates the search for "hidden" tree-like structures in formulas---for instance by detecting so-called weak $t$-treewidth backdoors. Such backdoors are sets of $k$ variables that can be assigned in such a way that the remaining instance has treewidth at most $t$ and is satisfiable whenever the original instance is.   Ever since Gaspers and Szeider [ICALP 2012] showed that finding a weak $t$-treewidth backdoor for a SAT formula is $\mathrm{W}[2]$-hard with respect to $k$, tractability results have been restricted to structurally sparse formulas---most notably, a linear-time algorithm for $d$-SAT (bounded clause-length SAT) by Fomin, Lokshtanov, Misra, Ramanujan, and Saurabh [SODA 2015] and a non-uniform polynomial-time algorithm when the incidence graph of the input formula belongs to a nowhere-dense graph class (or more generally is $K_{d,d}$-free) by Lokshtanov, Panolan, and Ramanujan [ICALP 2022].   In this paper, we push the tractability boundaries of finding weak $t$-treewidth backdoors beyond sparsity and into the regime of "well-behaved" dense formulas. Aiming towards relaxing structural input restrictions from nowhere-dense to edge-stable graph classes, as featured in the theory of beyond sparsity for FO model checking, or to bounded VC-dimension set systems, we identify signed semi-ladder-freeness as the correct dense structural restriction that establishes the boundary between tractability and intractability along this line.

title: Almost Optimal Relative Error Streaming Quantiles with Full Mergeability
abstract: Quantile summaries provide a scalable way to estimate the distribution of individual attributes in large datasets that are often distributed across multiple machines or generated by sensor networks. The state-of-the-art summaries with \emph{relative error guarantees} of $\pm \varepsilon\cdot \mathrm{rank}$, offering increasingly higher accuracy towards the distribution's tails, are ReqSketch (Cormode et al., JACM 2023) and the recent streaming algorithm by Gribelyuk et al. (SODA 2025). For inputs of size $N$ and probability $δ$ of exceeding the error bound, ReqSketch achieves space of $O(\varepsilon^{-1}\cdot \log^{1.5}(\varepsilon N)\cdot \sqrt{\log δ^{-1}})$ memory words, and offers \emph{full mergeability}, allowing distributed or parallel processing of datasets. In contrast, the latter algorithm exceeds the lower bound of $Ω(\varepsilon^{-1}\cdot \log(\varepsilon N)\cdot \log\logδ^{-1})$ from (Cormode \& Veselý, PODS 2020) only by a factor of $O(\log\varepsilon^{-1}\cdot (\log \varepsilon^{-1} + \log\log N)\cdot\log^2\logδ^{-1})$, but it lacks the mergeability property, is substantially more involved than ReqSketch, and has unclear practical performance. Both of these data structures consist of relative compactors from ReqSketch that subsample the stream in a structured way and work well in the streaming setting but are difficult to analyze under mergeability.   We design a new relative-error quantile summary that achieves full mergeability and also improves the state-of-the-art streaming space bound to $$O(\varepsilon^{-1}\cdot \log(\varepsilon N) \cdot\log \log δ^{-1} \cdot (\log \varepsilon^{-1} + \log \log(\varepsilon N) + \log \log δ^{-1})),$$ which is substantially closer to the lower bound. At the same time, our data structure is simpler than the algorithm from (Gribelyuk et al., SODA 2025) and therefore more suitable for implementation.

title: A Deterministic Near-Linear Time Approximation Algorithm for Restricted Shortest Paths in Directed Graphs
abstract: In the restricted shortest paths problem, we are given an $n$-vertex $m$-edge directed graph $G$ whose edges are assigned two non-negative weights (or resources) called lengths and costs, a source vertex $s$, and a cost threshold $C$. The goal is to find, for each target vertex $t$, the length of the shortest $(s,t)$-path whose total cost is at most $C$.   Ashvinkumar, Bernstein, and Karczmarz (SODA 2025) gave the first randomized bicriteria $(1+\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)$-approximate algorithm on directed graphs running in sub-$mn$ time, answering a problem posed by Bernstein (SODA 2012). We substantially improve this on two fronts, supplying a deterministic bicriteria $(1+\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)$-approximate algorithm running in near-linear time.   Our approach straightforwardly generalizes to more than two resources. For $k$ resources, a deterministic $(1+\varepsilon_1,\ldots,1+\varepsilon_k)$-approximate algorithm running in near-linear time is possible, with $\varepsilon_1=\ldots=\varepsilon_k=\varepsilon$.

title: The Complexity of Hamiltonian Cycles and Paths with Prescribed Walk Lengths
abstract: Fix a set $S$ of positive integers. An $S$-Hamiltonian cycle is a cyclic ordering of all vertices of a graph such that each consecutive pair is joined by a walk whose length belongs to $S$. We study the complexity of deciding whether an input graph admits such an ordering, together with the corresponding path variants with prescribed or unrestricted endpoints. We complete the complexity classification for undirected graphs. In particular, we prove NP-completeness for every finite nonempty set of odd lengths, resolving an open problem posed by Amarilli, Lombardo, and Monet (WG 2026). For digraphs, all three problems are NP-complete for every fixed finite nonempty $S$ and admit linear-time algorithms when $S$ is cofinite. For other fixed infinite sets $S$, we establish NP-complete and undecidable cases, with undecidability occurring even when $S$ is recursive.

title: No Truly Sublogarithmic-Round Algorithm for Distributed MIS in the LOCAL Model
abstract: We prove that $o(\frac{\log n}{\log\log n})$-round randomized LOCAL algorithms find a maximal independent set (MIS) with subconstant probability on some input. This shows that the 40-year-old $O(\log n)$-round randomized CONGEST algorithm of Luby and Alon, Babai, and Itai is nearly optimal. Our lower bound improves upon the $Ω(\sqrt{\log n})$-round lower bound of Khoury and Schild and nearly closes the 20+ year-old gap between the $O(\log n)$-round algorithm and the $Ω(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}})$-round lower bound of Kuhn, Moscibroda, and Wattenhofer.   To close this gap, one must show a lower bound for a graph that is not locally treelike. We do this by starting with a $D$-regular, $Θ(\log_D n)$-girth graph, with $D = Θ(\log n)$. Crucially, this is not our final graph. We obtain our hard instance by \emph{replacing} each vertex of this treelike graph with a clique on $n^c$ vertices for some constant $c \in (0,1)$. We then replace each edge with a bipartite Erdős--Rényi graph between the corresponding cliques, with each edge present independently with probability $1/2$.   We analyze arbitrary LOCAL algorithms on our non-treelike hard instance with a novel round elimination approach. We describe algorithms that output a set of vertices in this graph using two metrics: their \emph{occupancy probability} and their \emph{conflict probability}. Our round elimination framework takes an $r$-round algorithm and produces an $(r-1)$-round algorithm where occupancy and conflict probabilities collectively slightly degrade, but individually can significantly improve or degrade. This round elimination result is obtained by exploiting the lack of large biclique complements in dense bipartite Erdős--Rényi graphs, which in turn allows us to bound the entropy of the output distribution for any independent set algorithm.

title: A Better-than-2 Approximation for k-Median Part I: The Power of General Bids
abstract: The Greedy algorithm of Jain, Mahdian, Markakis, Saberi, and Vazirani was the best Lagrangian-multiplier-preserving (LMP) approximation algorithm for facility location, and thus the engine behind the best $k$-median guarantees, for over two decades. Its $2$-LMP guarantee was only recently broken by a small amount ($(2-η)$-LMP where $η\approx 2.25 \cdot 10^{-7}$) through local-search post-processing. That analysis relies on the structure of worst-case instances, and it appears difficult to obtain substantial further improvements along those lines.   We take a different approach and change the algorithm itself: we introduce general bidding functions, replacing the classical linear bid with a richer family of rules and prove a polynomial-time $1.95$-LMP approximation, a large improvement over the long-standing factor of~$2$.   We further show that these generalized bidding rules can be made smooth (log-adaptive), building on the recent framework developed for the classical Greedy algorithm by Cohen-Addad, Grandoni, Lee, Schwiegelshohn, and Svensson. This yields a polynomial-time $1.95$-approximation that opens $k+O_\varepsilon(\log n)$ centers. Combined with a $(1.89+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm for stable instances in our companion work \cite{stableinstances}, we achieve a better-than-2 approximation for the $k$-median problem in polynomial-time.

title: On the Parameterized Complexity of Capacitated Stack and Queue Layouts with Colored Edges
abstract: Stack and queue layouts are two extensively studied and complementary linear representations of graphs. A stack (queue) layout $\langle \prec, σ\rangle$ of a graph $G$ consists of a total ordering $\prec$ of its vertices and of a partitioning $σ$ of its edges into pages, such that no two independent edges on the same page cross (nest). We propose a generalized model with colored edges (one color per edge) and capacitated pages. Namely, the input graph is equipped with colored edges and a prescribed budget for each page-color pair $(p,c)$ - this budget determines the maximum number of edges of color $c$ that page $p$ can accept. This model is motivated by fair allocation scenarios where budgets can be used to control the share of monochromatic edges on each page. Unfortunately, it is known that deciding whether a stack (queue) layout exists is NP-hard already with two (one) pages. Thus, we focus on the fixed-order setting - where the linear order $\prec$ is part of the input - for which an ordinary 2-page stack or $\ell$-page queue layout can be computed in polynomial time. Despite the restrictive setting, we show that both capacitated problems are NP-complete already for two pages. Furthermore, we study the complexity of the problems when parameterized by the number of pages, colors, and/or the structure of the edge conflict graph with respect to the fixed linear order $\prec$. Our analysis paints a detailed complexity landscape and uncovers a surprisingly intricate interplay between the considered parameters.

title: Exact power indices for plurality-voting ensembles
abstract: Plurality-voting ensembles aggregate the predictions of multiple base classifiers and output the most voted class, with ties typically broken at random. Despite the simple aggregation rule, attributing the impact of each base classifier to the ensemble's predictions is far from straightforward. That is, a single base classifier's impact depends on how it interacts with the votes of all other classifiers in the ensemble, for example, in resolving ties, and not only on its own predictions. We address the attribution problem using established tools from cooperative game theory, studying the Banzhaf and Shapley power indices for new games modeling plurality voting and random tie-breaking, for binary and multiclass classification settings. Computing power indices is, in general, intractable. Surprisingly, our methods, collectively named ENPOWER, enable the exact computation of Banzhaf and Shapley values in linear time for the binary classification setting and in low-degree polynomial time for the multiclass setting. The algorithms in ENPOWER rely on new combinatorial formulations of the Banzhaf and Shapley indices, yielding closed-form solutions for the binary case and ordinary generating function representations for the multiclass case. We validate empirically the methods in ENPOWER demonstrating their high applicability, providing attribution values not captured by existing methods. We apply the attribution of ENPOWER to: ensemble pruning and prompt-based ensembling of vision-language models.

title: Mining Correlated Motifs with Wildcards in PPI Networks: Exact and Optimal
abstract: A protein-protein interaction (PPI) network is a graph whose nodes are protein sequences and whose edges represent physical interactions between proteins. Correlated Motif Mining (CMM) seeks pairs of sequence motifs whose co-occurrence in interacting proteins reveals binding sites and interaction mechanisms. Formally, in the $(\ell,d)$-CMM problem, we are given a graph $G=(V,E)$, with $V\subseteqΣ^*$ for an alphabet $Σ$, and integers $0\leq d<\ell$, and we seek a pair $\{X,Y\}$ of motifs, each of length $\ell$ and containing $d$ wildcards, that maximizes a support measure $f(G,\{X,Y\})$; e.g., the count $f_E$ of edges $\{u,v\}\in E$ such that $X$ matches a substring of $u$ and $Y$ matches a substring of $v$, or vice versa. Although existing approaches have produced biologically meaningful results, they are either inefficient or heuristic-based, as the underlying optimization problem is NP-hard.   Here, we revisit $(\ell,d)$-CMM. For $d=0$, we give an exact $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$-time and $\mathcal{O}(N)$-space algorithm, where $N$ is the total length of the node strings, and prove that this time is conditionally optimal under the Strong Exponential-Time Hypothesis. For any $d>0$, we give an exact $\mathcal{O}\!\left(\binom{\ell}{d}^2N^2\right)$-time and $\mathcal{O}(N)$-space algorithm, and observe that the problem is W[1]-hard parameterized by $d$. The latter algorithm improves the state of the art by exponentially large factors in both time and space. We further demonstrate experimentally that our algorithms are practical on real-world PPI networks and find significantly higher-scoring motif pairs than the state of the art. Moreover, we show that our algorithms find many top-scoring motif pairs that the state of the art misses entirely. Taken together, our results suggest that exact CMM with wildcards is more tractable in practice than previously assumed.

title: Jumbled Simon's Equivalence and Embeddings
abstract: \emph{Jumbled scattered factors} are a generalisation of scattered factors (or subsequences) where a jumbled scattered factor is obtained from another word by deleting and rearranging letters. For limiting the number of rearrangements, we distinguish $\ell$-jumbled scattered factors where $\ell$ limits the number of letters that may occur rearranged. For instance, $\mathtt{car}$, $\mathtt{start}$, $\mathtt{rat}, \mathtt{cat}$ are jumbled scattered factors of $\mathtt{abstract}$ even though $\mathtt{car}$, $\mathtt{start}$ and $\mathtt{cat}$ are no scattered factors and each need one jumble. An example for a jumbled scattered factor with $2$ jumbles is $\mathtt{tatar}$. In this work, we investigate two problems on jumbled scattered factors from an algorithmic perspective. First, we give algorithms for testing jumbled Simon's equivalence where two words are equivalent if they share the same $\ell$-jumbled scattered factors up to length $k$. Second, we investigate how to count the possible occurrences of a jumbled scattered factor -- the jumbled binomial coefficient. After defining the jumbled binomial coefficient, we study jumbled embeddings and factorisations of such as well.

title: PHastR: Faster Minimal Perfect Hashing with Rotated Layouts
abstract: We present PHastR, a minimal perfect hash function of the PHast family. Like PHast+, the fast-to-build variant of PHast, PHastR finds feasible seeds with bit-parallel operations: its seeds move keys along rings of slots, and to evaluate the seeds of a bucket it cyclically shifts, for each key, a word recording which slots of its ring are used. Unlike PHast+, however, it avoids self-collisions, which make two keys of a bucket collide for (almost) all its seeds: more than a third of the buckets bumped by PHast+ with wrapping and multiplier 3 contain one. With 8-bit seeds, PHastR uses $1.94$ bits per key, the same space as the best variant of PHast+ with wrapping, but it is built in $37\%$ of the time, and its queries are $28\%$ faster on $10^9$ keys, as it bumps $0.5\%$ of the keys instead of $3.9\%$; they are faster also than those of PHast, which takes eleven times as long to build, and about as fast as those of PtrHash, which uses more than one bit per key more. With a larger expected bucket size PHastR comes within $0.02$ bits per key of the space of PHast, using $1.90$ bits per key, and still has faster queries. Its construction also scales better with the number of threads: with all the threads of a 48-core machine it is almost three times faster than that of PHast+. Finally, we argue that when each key can be placed only within a range of $W$ slots, every placement of $n$ random keys on $n$ slots, however found, must bump on large key sets a constant fraction of the keys: we derive a lower bound of about $0.1/W$ on this fraction, and we estimate that the best placement bumps about $1/2W$ of the keys, which is about on tenth of the keys bumped by PHastR.

title: A Matroid Generalization of Weighted Popular Matching: Characterization and Algorithm
abstract: We study a problem that unifies two major generalizations of popular matchings in the one-sided preference model. In a bipartite graph in which each vertex, or applicant, on one side has preferences over the adjacent vertices, a matching is called popular if it does not lose a head-to-head election against any other matching. Since the seminal work of Abraham, Irving, Kavitha, and Mehlhorn, who gave the first polynomial-time algorithm for finding a popular matching, numerous generalizations of the popular matching problem have been investigated. Two prominent directions are weighted popular matchings, in which each applicant is assigned a voting weight, and popularity problems under matroid constraints. The former admits a polynomial-time algorithm due to Mestre, while the most general form of the latter is the popular common independent set problem, for which a polynomial-time algorithm is given by Kavitha, Makino, Schlotter, and Yokoi.   In this paper, we introduce the weighted popular common independent set problem, which simultaneously generalizes weighted popular matchings and popular common independent sets. Our main result is the first polynomial-time algorithm for this problem. A key ingredient of the algorithm is a solution-independent characterization of weighted popular common independent sets, which we establish in this paper. As consequences of our algorithmic result, we obtain polynomial-time algorithms for several previously unresolved problems, including weighted popular matchings with matroid constraints and weighted popular branchings.

title: Sampling from the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick Model up to Criticality
abstract: We prove that the simulated annealing algorithm efficiently samples from the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model at inverse temperature $β< 1$ to an arbitrary inverse polynomial accuracy in total variation.

title: Fully Dynamic Random-Walk Quantities on Undirected Expanders and $κ$-Uniform Directed Graphs
abstract: We study fully dynamic data structures for random-walk quantities on undirected expanders and fast-mixing directed graphs. For an unweighted graph whose normalized Laplacian has spectral gap at least $γ$, we give a $(1\pm\varepsilon)$ effective-resistance data structure with expected update time $O(γ^{-4}\varepsilon^{-2}\log n\log^4(n/\varepsilon))$ and expected $O(1)$ query time.   For directed graphs, somewhat surprisingly, the OMv conjecture precludes a fast data structure based on rapid mixing conditions alone. To address this, we introduce the notion of $κ$-uniform directed graphs, which requires the stationary distribution to $κ$-approximate the uniform distribution, and show that in this setting, random walk based data structures with $\text{poly}(κ, \log{n}, \varepsilon^{-1})$ update/query times are possible.

title: Hitting Minors: Stronger Lower Bounds
abstract: For a fixed finite collection of graphs $\mathcal{F}$, the $\mathcal{F}$-Minor-Free Deletion problem asks, given a graph $G$ and an integer $k$, whether there is a set $S\subseteq V(G)$ with $|S|\leq k$ such that $G-S$ contains no graph of $\mathcal{F}$ as a minor. This generalizes Vertex Cover, Feedback Vertex Set, and Vertex Planarization, among many others. Baste, Sau, and Thilikos [JCSS 2020, SICOMP 2023] showed that, assuming the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), there are collections $\mathcal{F}$ for which the problem cannot be solved in time $2^{o(\mathrm{tw}\log\mathrm{tw})}n^{O(1)}$ on $n$-vertex graphs of treewidth $\mathrm{tw}$, and gave a matching algorithm.   We ask whether this super-exponential dependence persists under more restrictive structural parameters. First, we strengthen their lower bound. Assuming ETH, for every fixed $h\geq 6$, $\{P_h\}$-Minor-Free Deletion, where $P_h$ is the path on $h$ vertices, cannot be solved in time $2^{o(t\log t)}n^{O(1)}$, where $t=\mathrm{fvs}+\mathrm{td}$ is the sum of the feedback vertex set number and treedepth of the input graph. These two parameters are incomparable, but both individually upper bound the treewidth. Together with the $2^{O(\mathrm{tw}\log\mathrm{tw})}n^{O(1)}$-time algorithm of Baste, Sau, and Thilikos [SICOMP 2023], our lower bound is tight.   In contrast, we show that asymptotically faster algorithms are possible when parameterized by the vertex cover number $\mathrm{vc}$. Specifically, for any finite family $\mathcal{F}$, $\mathcal{F}$-Minor-Free Deletion can be solved in time $2^{O(\mathrm{vc})}n^{O(1)}$. Taken together, our results show that the boundary between single-exponential and super-exponential complexity for this problem lies between the vertex cover number and the feedback vertex set number (plus treedepth).

title: Nearly Optimal Quantum Sample Complexity of Learning Fourier-Sparse Boolean Functions
abstract: We study the number of uniform quantum examples needed to exactly learn a Boolean function with at most $k$ nonzero Fourier coefficients. We give a learner with near-optimal $\widetilde{O}(k)$ sample complexity independent of the input length $n$. The learner uses only separate measurements of individual examples. This improves the previous $O(k^{3/2}\log^2 k)$ upper bound (Arunachalam, Chakraborty, Lee, Paraashar, and de Wolf, 2021). The main ingredient is a candidate set formed by symmetric differences of subsets from independent groups of Fourier samples. A multilinear majority polynomial combines unbiased random approximations into an accurate witness whose Fourier support lies in this set. Granularity then forces the set to contain the entire Fourier support, including subsets never directly sampled. For comparison, we derive the tight classical sample complexity $Θ(nk)$ by combining known sparse-recovery and lower-bound results.

title: Query Complexity of Densest Sub(hyper)graph Problems
abstract: Rubinstein et al. introduce the study of connectivity and minimum cut problems in the cut query model, where an algorithm can only access the edges of a graph through CUT queries. In this work, we examine the query complexity of densest subgraph problems. Our first contribution is to generalize the uniform sparsification approach for Densest Subgraph and other heavy subgraph problems to weighted graphs, achieving the following results.   >A $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for weighted Densest Subgraph in $O(n\log^2 n/\varepsilon^2)$ queries, roughly matching the $Ω(n/\log n)$ lower bound we prove for randomized algorithms.   >A $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for weighted Max Cut in $O(n\log^2 n/\varepsilon^2)$ queries. This improves upon the bound of $O(n\log^3 n(\log n+1/\varepsilon^2))$ queries achieved by Plevrakis et al., making significant progress towards their lower bound of $Ω(n/\log n)$ queries.   In contrast, we rule out approximation schemes with truly subquadratic query complexity for Densest $k$-Subgraph and settle its exact query complexity in both the unweighted and deterministic settings.   For hypergraphs, we show CUT queries alone cannot achieve $o(\sqrt{n})$-approximation for Densest Subhypergraph or $o(n)$-approximation for Densest $k$-Subhypergraph, regardless of the number of queries. Augmenting CUT queries with the EDGE oracle of Chen et al., we overcome this barrier for Densest Subhypergraph and obtain a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation on rank-$r$ hypergraphs using $O(nr\log n/\varepsilon^2)$ queries. We also extend our Densest $k$-Subgraph hardness results to hypergraphs and prove exponential query lower bounds for exact Densest $k$-Subhypergraph. Lastly, confirming a conjecture of Chakrabarty and Liao, we show that simulating an ADD query using CUT and IS-EDGE$^?$ queries requires exponentially-many queries.

title: Certifying Capacity and Gaps of the Rank-Dependent Gain-Sharing Framework for Ranking
abstract: The randomized primal-dual framework of Devanur, Jain, and Kleinberg (SODA 2013) splits each unit matching gain between endpoint dual variables according to the matched offline rank. The gain-sharing function affects the certificate but not Ranking's decisions. Keeping the splitting rule and expected edgewise feasibility criterion fixed, we define certifying capacity as the strongest uniform guarantee obtainable by functional optimization over a prescribed function class. Its shortfall from Ranking's actual competitiveness is the certifying gap.   We study unweighted online bipartite matching under adversarial arrivals on graphs with online degree at most $d$ and on $d$-regular graphs. The optimized protocol is tight on both degree-one classes and in the unrestricted setting, but has a strictly positive gap on both degree-two classes, even over all measurable nonnegative complementary splits. In both degree-two settings, we determine Ranking's exact competitiveness and the exact certifying capacity over nondecreasing gain-sharing functions. For general $d$, we optimize over nondecreasing, right-continuous functions $f:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ with $f(1)=1$, using their probability-measure representation. Both the certifying capacity and actual competitiveness converge to $1-1/e$ in both instance families as $d\to\infty$. The resulting gap is at most $1/(2ed)+O(d^{-2})$ for online degree at most $d$; on $d$-regular graphs, it vanishes but is at least $(1/(2e)-o(1))/d$. These results distinguish function-class restrictions from limitations of the fixed protocol and motivate tighter randomized primal-dual frameworks.

title: Improved Combinatorial Auctions with and without Samples
abstract: We give new mechanisms for combinatorial auctions in the offline, secretary, and prophet-with-samples models. Specifically, we obtain the following guarantees for social welfare maximization with $m$ items and $n$ XOS buyers:   * In the prophet-with-samples version, buyers arrive in adversarial order and draw their values from independent distributions. We give a universally truthful, polynomial-time $(2+\eps)$-approximation mechanism using $O(\log\!\log m)$ samples from each distribution. The approximation factor is tight even for a single item and without the incentive constraints, due to the classic prophet inequality. Compared to the previous state-of-the-art with the same guarantees [Dütting--Kesselheim--Lucier--Reiffenhäuser--Singla (FOCS 2024)], our running time is exponentially faster, and our sample complexity is doubly-exponentially lower, resolving two explicit open problems by Dütting et al.   * Using the same techniques, we also obtain improved mechanisms in the secretary and offline versions, where the values are worst-case, and buyers are processed in either random order (secretary) or without any timing restrictions (offline). After a long line of works, the state of the art in both models is an $O((\log\!\log m)^2)$-approximation due to [Assadi--Kesselheim--Singla (SODA 2021)], who explicitly ask whether it can be improved to $O(\log\!\log m)$. We indeed obtain an $O(\log\!\log m)$-approximate universally truthful mechanism for the secretary and offline models.

title: Joint Neural Posterior Estimation and Model Selection for Chemical Reaction Networks
abstract: Simulation-based Bayesian inference for Chemical Reaction Networks (CRNs) must simultaneously solve two computationally demanding problems: discriminating between overlapping reaction pathways and estimating reaction rate constants. Classical approaches, such as Sequential Monte Carlo ABC, rely on handcrafted summary statistics and scale poorly across large parameter spaces. To overcome this, we introduce a neural inference architecture. Our pipeline utilizes shared 1D-CNNs and a permutation-invariant Set Attention mechanism to learn low-dimensional summary statistics from variable-length, multi-experiment time-series data. These statistics simultaneously condition a model selection network to compute posterior model probabilities and model-specific conditional Invertible Neural Networks (cINNs) that estimate parameter posterior distributions. We demonstrate the practical utility of our approach on a real protodeboronation example, illustrating how it handles structural ambiguity and extracts kinetic parameters from competing catalyst deactivation pathways.

title: Designing for Prediction: Planning Formulas for Expected Out-of-Sample $R^2$ and $r$
abstract: Design calculations let researchers gauge, before data is collected, whether a planned study is likely to detect an effect. In this paper, we develop such calculations for predictive models using ordinary least squares and ridge regression under leave-one-out cross-validation. To do so, we derive closed-form expressions relating the expected out-of-sample $R^2$ and the expected correlation between observed and predicted outcomes to four design-stage quantities: sample size, number of predictors, an assumed population $R^2$ ($ρ^2_{in}$) and a design efficiency factor $D^*$ (which summarizes how leverage is distributed across observations). Unlike the classical shrinkage formulas, which depend only on sample size and dimension, these are sensitive to how covariates are arranged -- to imbalance and skew. A simulation study assesses the accuracy of the formulas against realized values under a variety of data generating mechanisms. We apply the methods to a published study predicting personality from smartphone behavior and show that the design formulas would have indicated, before any analyses were run, that least squares could not be expected to beat the sample mean while ridge could. An R package, predpower, implements the calculations.

title: From Fourier Amplitudes to Persistence Images for Impact-Echo Defect Detection
abstract: Impact-echo testing is a nondestructive testing method used to detect internal defects in concrete structures. However, boundary reflections, structured interference, and measurement noise can produce complex Fourier amplitude spectra, making defect classification difficult. We constructed a two-dimensional frequency--amplitude persistence image (FA-PI) from the Fourier amplitude spectrum. Using a fixed parameterization of exact multi-parameter persistent homology, each retained Fourier component is represented with frequency-bin location as one coordinate and amplitude as the other, and Gaussian kernels are then applied in this two-dimensional space. This construction has a direct analytical connection to the corresponding one-dimensional Gaussian-smoothed Fourier amplitude spectrum. FA-PI was evaluated on an experimental backfill-void dataset and a public bridge-deck impact-echo dataset, and compared with raw and Gaussian-smoothed Fourier amplitude spectra using a linear classifier with a Softmax output and identical signal-level data splits. The evaluation included original signals and signals corrupted by Gaussian noise, sinusoidal interference, or mixed noise, with matching noise types and signal-to-noise ratios during training, validation, and testing. Performance was assessed using accuracy and macro-averaged precision, recall, and F1-score. Across the two datasets, FA-PI consistently outperformed the raw and Gaussian-smoothed Fourier baselines in the noisy-condition summaries. These findings indicate that representing Fourier spectral components in a two-dimensional frequency--amplitude space can improve impact-echo defect classification beyond frequency-axis smoothing alone.

title: BridgeTwist: Twisting Schrödinger Bridges for Training-Free Conditional Sampling
abstract: Generative models are often required to serve many downstream conditional tasks. In the training-free setting, a pretrained unconditional model is reused as a prior and combined with a task-specific likelihood to sample from the corresponding posterior. While such training-free samplers have been developed for diffusion and flow models, their counterpart for Schrödinger bridge (SB) models remains unexplored, despite the growing appeal of SBs as flexible stochastic transport models between general source and target distributions. We propose BridgeTwist, a training-free conditional sampler for pretrained SB generative models, formulated as a tempered twisted sequential Monte Carlo scheme. Its twist is a closed-form plug-in surrogate, obtained by combining the velocity and score fields exposed by SB pretraining into an endpoint predictor and evaluating the likelihood there. Since this surrogate is less reliable near the source, we temper the twist with a time-varying exponent, downweighting its influence at early steps. We further introduce a bridge-shaped inference-time diffusion schedule that concentrates the proposal noise in the interior of the path. Telescoping importance weights then cancel all intermediate twist factors, yielding an asymptotically exact sampler for the posterior. Empirically, BridgeTwist outperforms training-free baselines on class-conditional and text-prompted image generation, and is competitive with specialized inverse problem solvers on inpainting, deblurring, and super-resolution.

title: Minimax rates for pointwise CATE estimation: the role of design smoothness
abstract: We study the role of design smoothness in the minimax estimation of conditional average treatment effects at a fixed covariate point. For design densities bounded above and away from zero, without further regularity, we derive upper and lower risk bounds with an arbitrarily small gap in the convergence-rate exponent. Under uniform design, we obtain matching upper and lower bounds at interior points in the regime of low nuisance smoothness. These results show that rough covariate designs can lead to slower rates than uniform designs, even under the same smoothness assumptions on the treatment effect and nuisance functions, highlighting the role of the covariate distribution in pointwise causal estimation.

title: Understanding Circulant Permutation to Extend the CMinHash Estimator
abstract: CMinHash promises a new direction for designing MinHash algorithms with reduced variance and storage space via circulant permutations. However, the original variance analysis is difficult to extend to other MinHash estimators. We present a new approach that gives explicit and easily comparable approximate variance expressions, and use it to analyze the Minner estimator. Numerical experiments show that our variance expression matches the empirical mean square error (MSE) of estimates. Our work thereby demonstrates how to apply circulant permutation to other MinHash estimators and compute their approximate variance.

title: Two For The Price Of One: Curvature-Aware Pruning Preserves Influence Functions Too
abstract: Post-training pruning enables efficient deployment, but conventional methods do not explicitly preserve internal-gradient alignment between sparse and dense models. We study novel connections between downstream performance of compressed models and the ability to retain gradient information via influence-function preservation. Central to this connection is a curvature-aware objective that accounts for both layer activations and backpropagated gradients. Despite its promise, this objective remains underexplored in pruning due to a lack of efficient solvers. We introduce $\texttt{CACTUS}$, a novel ADMM-based optimizer supporting both pruning and sparse-plus-low-rank decompositions of pre-trained weights.
