In both cases, we observe systematic miscalibration for aggregation models such as Majority Vote, Dawid--Skene, GLAD, and CrowdFM. Finally, we propose a post-hoc calibration procedure that \emph{aggregates the aggregators}: for any aggregation function $φ$, we introduce a transformation that first combines its predictive distribution with those of complementary aggregators, before applying temperature scaling. This simple and interpretable transformation makes temperature scaling more effective than when applied directly to $φ$. It improves calibration, especially in the high-redundancy regime where there are many annotations per item, while generally preserving or even improving accuracy.

title: Multi-Day Stochastic Dispatch for Power Systems With Long-Duration Storage Using Diffusion-Generated Weather Forecasts
abstract: As power systems shift toward high shares of wind and solar, long-duration storage becomes pivotal for balancing multi-day deficits and surpluses of uncertain supply and demand. Current dispatch strategies for long-duration storage either assign a fixed value to stored energy or extend the modeled horizon using a single forecast. Stochastic system dispatch with a multi-day horizon for long-duration storage remains unexplored, and existing stochastic dispatch only considers day-ahead uncertainty or Markovian uncertainty beyond one week of perfect foresight. Therefore, we benchmark stochastic multi-day dispatch against deterministic alternatives in a rolling-horizon setup. To emulate probabilistic multi-day forecasts, we combine diffusion with a semi-Markov model of weather regimes and a logistic growth model for meteorological forecast errors. At high renewable shares, stochastic operation reduces thermal backup generation and consistently eliminates loss of load. The benefits decrease with smaller shares of renewables, less long-duration storage, or higher forecast skill. Overall, our results suggest that systems with high shares of variable renewables can substantially benefit from probabilistic multi-day forecasts and stochastic dispatch.

title: Input-Constrained Active Disturbance Rejection Control for AUVs
abstract: This paper addresses the control of autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) operating in dynamic environments, where wave-induced forces, modelling errors, and actuator limitations make reliable control challenging. Active disturbance rejection control (ADRC), together with an extended state observer (ESO), estimates lumped uncertainties online, simplifying control design using nominal models. However, existing stability analyses typically assume bounded control inputs and derivatives, which are difficult to guarantee under unknown disturbances and measurement noise. To bridge this theory--practice gap, this paper introduces an ADRC framework with active input saturation and post-saturation low-pass filtering. The saturation constrains the control magnitude, while the filter regularizes the saturated signal to ensure bounded input-rate variations. By explicitly enforcing these conditions, the proposed system guarantees semi-global practical asymptotic stability. High-fidelity simulations and experiments on an underwater robotic platform demonstrate robust control performance under severe environmental disturbances and actuator constraints. A supplementary video is available at https://youtu.be/AEFlZ69Yg00.

title: From Orbit Matching to Docking: A Hierarchical Reinforcement-Learning Approach to Multiphase Rendezvous Trajectory Design
abstract: As the complexity of space missions increases, autonomous spacecraft guidance must accommodate transitions between mission phases with distinct dynamics, objectives, and constraints. Rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) are particularly challenging because they span multiple operating regimes, from orbital-scale matching and far-range approach to close-range maneuvering and terminal docking. Existing reinforcement-learning approaches generally address only a subset of this sequence or rely on manually defined switching conditions between controllers. This study presents a hierarchical reinforcement-learning framework for autonomous, three-degree-of-freedom RPO that spans the complete trajectory from orbit matching to docking. Five specialized policies are trained for orbit matching, far-range approach, mid-range approach, close-range approach, and docking. A learned high-level manager policy then selects among these phase-specific controllers based on the evolving spacecraft state. The hierarchical approach is evaluated over the full end-to-end rendezvous sequence and compared with a fixed sequential-invocation heuristic to assess trajectory performance and transition behavior. Training and inference metrics are also analyzed for the individual phase policies and the complete hierarchical system.

title: Model-Based Cortisol Replacement Strategies for Patients With Adrenal Insufficiency
abstract: Cortisol is an essential hormone secreted by the adrenal glands. Abnormally low level of cortisol is referred to as adrenal insufficiency. This paper focuses on devising treatment strategies for patients suffering from adrenal insufficiency using a model-based approach. Two conditions of adrenal insufficiency are analysed. They are hypothalamic-pituitary (HP) and adrenal gland disorders. The hypothalamus, pituitary, and adrenal glands constitute the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, which regulates stress and maintains physiological homeostasis through cortisol secretion. A comparative analysis of the existing mathematical models of the HPA axis is conducted. Based on this analysis, a novel model of the HPA axis is proposed that incorporates endogenous circadian rhythm. This proposed model is used to design effective cortisol replacement strategies. In addition, hydrocortisone replacement therapies are proposed and validated with clinical data from the literature. The results presented in this paper are applicable to patient-specific treatment strategies for individuals with adrenal insufficiency.

title: Direct Electromechanical Actuation of the Shift Drum in Non-Synchronized Motorcycle Transmissions: From Actuator Sizing and Electronics Design to Closed-Loop Position Control
abstract: This thesis presents the direct electromechanical actuation of the shift drum in a non-synchronized motorcycle transmission. A DC motor drives the shift drum through a self-locking worm gear, so the entire foot shift mechanism is eliminated. As a reference, 84 manual gear changes of a large-displacement series-production motorcycle were measured on a chassis dynamometer; the mean shift time is 80 ms for upshifts and 92 ms for downshifts. The system design covers the complete chain from the mechanics to the software. The actuator motor is sized from inertia, friction and gear ratio. A dedicated shift controller is developed with supply filtering, signal conditioning for the position sensor and the incremental encoder, an H-bridge motor driver and a custom circuit board based on a SAMD21 microcontroller. The embedded firmware implements position control of the shift drum with a proportional controller, without inner speed or current loops. On a gearbox test rig, a gear change is completed in less than 80 ms without overshoot in a single measurement, below the mean of the manual reference shifts. The analysis reveals a trade-off in the choice of the worm gear ratio: at a ratio of 30, about 93% of the motor torque is needed to accelerate the motor shaft and the worm. A ratio of about 8 halves the required torque, but the worm gear then loses its self-locking. The measured shift times are published as an open dataset.

title: Filtering for Liveness: Recurrence via Backup Reachability Control Barrier Functions
abstract: Liveness requires a dynamical system to repeatedly accomplish a desired objective over time. In this work, we consider a particular form of liveness known as recurrence, which requires the closed-loop trajectory to regularly revisit a prescribed set, with no more than a specified amount of time between visits. Inspired by the control barrier function (CBF) safety-filter paradigm, we develop a controller-filtering framework that makes adjustments to a nominal controller only when necessary to guarantee recurrence. Unlike conventional CBF methods, which enforce set forward invariance, our framework allows the trajectory to leave the set while guaranteeing its timely return. To achieve this, our framework combines two components: a backup reachability CBF that preserves the ability to return to the prescribed set within the allowable time, and a timing-based mechanism that invokes a reaching controller only when the nominal behavior would otherwise fail to meet the return-time requirement. The resulting framework guarantees recurrence while preserving the nominal behavior when possible, enabling control objectives that require temporary excursions from the set, such as traversal between disjoint regions. Our method is successfully utilized in a drone racing example with a recurrence constraint on beacon visibility.

title: STATCOM-Based Flicker Mitigation in Electric Arc Furnace Systems Using DQ-PI and Lyapunov-Based Nonlinear Control
abstract: Electric arc furnaces inject stochastic reactive-power swings that cause voltage flicker at the point of common coupling. This paper compares two STATCOM inner controllers for an 11~kV, 50~Hz furnace feeder: a split-frequency DQ-PI design and a Lyapunov-based nonlinear design whose integral state is retained in the storage function, giving global asymptotic stability of the nominal unsaturated current-error subsystem. Gains for both controllers were tuned by a frozen metaheuristic campaign and then evaluated over 600~s with an IEC~61000-4-15 digital flickermeter. A post-campaign audit showed that the stochastic arc realization used for the original comparison was periodic, so the two selected gain sets were frozen without retuning or reselection and evaluated on ten independent stochastic realizations that had been specified and archived before the STO-ENS validation campaign, together with a paired uncompensated case for each realization. Both controllers reduce the mean short-term flicker severity by about 62% relative to the STO-ENS uncompensated baseline, and no statistically detectable difference in mean flicker severity is found between them. They separate instead in realization sensitivity: the Lyapunov standard deviation across arcs is roughly one third that of DQ-PI. Controller ordering inferred from a single stochastic trajectory is therefore not a reliable measure of stochastic robustness, and ensemble validation is necessary.

title: Reach-Avoid Certificates for Contact-based Stochastic Hybrid Systems
abstract: This work studies certified reach-avoid control of stochastic hybrid systems in which a stochastic differential equation governs continuous flow and a controlled stochastic kernel governs guard-triggered resets. The input appears only in the reset kernel, where it determines the post-jump distribution. Certificates for such systems have so far assumed spontaneous or controller-chosen jump times, a finite horizon, or discrete-time dynamics; we certify, over the infinite horizon, that the target is reached before the unsafe set with at least a prescribed probability. First, we introduce reach-avoid contact certificates, whose flow and jump conditions are imposed only on a sublevel corridor, and prove that any such certificate with a compatible reset policy meets the specification; a pointwise safety filter extends this guarantee from verification to control by constraining arbitrary nominal controllers. Next, we prove that executions are non-Zeno and bound the expected settling time and reset count. We frame certificate search as a linear program over any twice-differentiable dictionary followed by independent verification. We illustrate our approach via comparisons where the certified region is a subset covering 93.6\% of the ground truth and where our certificate-based safety filter reaches the goal while reducing collisions from 68 to zero across 200 episodes of a dribbling ball problem.

title: Stabilizing Low-Stiffness Soft Robots at Unstable Equilibria: A Model-Based Optimal Control Approach
abstract: Continuum soft robots are highly nonlinear and underactuated systems, which makes stabilizing them around unstable equilibrium points difficult. This challenge becomes even greater in low stiffness regimes, where gravitational forces dominate elastic forces. In this letter, we explore whether optimal control can address these challenges using a computa- tionally efficient method suitable for real time use. We propose a nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) approach based on Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP), combined with an accurate reduced order Variable Strain model with analytical derivatives. This results in an efficient control framework for addressing the stabilization problem. Tested on a soft inverted pendulum and other hybrid soft rigid systems, the method outperforms traditional controllers, stabilizes more challenging configurations, and operates reliably at real time speeds (50 150 Hz), demonstrating both effectiveness and practical feasibility in experimental settings.

title: Safety-Aware Dimension Selection for Reduced-Order Model Predictive Control
abstract: Model reduction can substantially reduce the computational burden of model predictive control (MPC) for high-dimensional systems, but a reduced dimension chosen for performance may be insufficient for safety-critical operation. This paper introduces a safety-aware dimension-selection framework in which the prediction model adapts to the order of the model required to maintain a certified finite-horizon safety condition. Dynamic active subspaces provide a performance-oriented ordering of reduced coordinates, while finite-horizon error bounds robustly enforce discrete-time control barrier function constraints. The controller selects the smallest prediction order for which the resulting safety-critical MPC problem remains feasible. We establish full-order horizon safety, recursive feasibility, and closed-loop invariance of the safe set under the proposed reduced-order formulation. The proposed approach therefore adapts the prediction complexity to safety requirements, avoiding unnecessary high-dimensional prediction during benign operation.

title: Reduced-Order Backstepping Control of Nonlinear Mechanical Systems with Input Delay via Galerkin Projection
abstract: This paper addresses trajectory tracking for a class of nonlinear mechanical systems with input delay. The delayed actuator channel is represented as an equivalent transport partial differential equation, thereby transforming the original delayed system into a coupled plant-channel representation. A finite-dimensional approximation of the delay channel is then constructed through Galerkin projection, resulting in an explicit ODE model of the delayed actuator dynamics. Using this reduced-order plant-channel model, a backstepping controller is developed, and Lyapunov analysis establishes uniform exponential stability of the nominal tracking error dynamics for the reduced-order Galerkin model. To enhance practical implementation, a command-filtered version is also introduced to avoid direct differentiation of virtual controls, for which a corresponding uniform ultimate boundedness result is obtained. Simulation studies are provided to validate the proposed design and illustrate the effectiveness of the method.

title: Coordinated Conservation Voltage Reduction and Network Topology Reconfiguration in Active Distribution Networks
abstract: Distribution networks rely on conservation voltage reduction (CVR) and network topology reconfiguration (NTR) to manage demand, distributed energy resources (DERs), and tighter operating margins. Yet these strategies are typically deployed independently, despite coupled effects on feeder voltages, losses, and loading. This paper addresses that gap by developing a day-ahead mixed-integer second order cone programming (MISOCP) framework that jointly optimizes feeder head voltage control and network reconfiguration. The formulation incorporates AC branch flow constraints, ZIP load models, DERs, battery energy storage systems, and multi substation radiality. Using modified IEEE 33 bus and 123 bus systems, four configurations isolate the individual and coordinated effects of CVR and NTR. On the 33-bus system under mixed ZIP loading, NTR reduces active energy loss by 2.50%, while coordinated operation reduces it by 2.91% relative to SDN and produces a 2.46% CVR induced active load reduction relative to SDNTR. Under constant impedance loading, coordinated operation reduces active energy loss by 17.65% relative to SDN, while CVR reduces active load by 14.61% relative to SDNTR. DER portfolio scaling shows a nonmonotonic coordinated load reduction response, strongest at 20% penetration and decreasing at higher levels. On the 123 bus system, NTR reduces losses by 19.3%, while CVR reduces voltage dependent load energy by 2.3 to 2.4%. Under loading stress, SDN becomes infeasible at 120% loading, whereas CEDNTR remains feasible. Overall, the results demonstrate complementary, operating condition dependent benefits shaped by load composition, DER portfolio scaling, feeder topology, voltage margins, and source constraints, highlighting the value of joint optimization.

title: When LLM Agents See a Conflict but Still Proceed: Cross-Domain Dependencies in Network Slicing
abstract: Future AI-native networks are being designed to apply autonomous agents built on large language models (LLMs) in network management through intents. When intents from different domains meet on the same resource, an agent must recognize the cross-domain dependency before taking an irreversible action. We investigate this problem through a smart-grid use case, in which a power utility holds an active intent on a backup slice for protection traffic. This slice appears idle by design, which is precisely the profile targeted by a cost-reduction intent. We built a tool-based environment in which the dependency must be either queried by the agent or read from an inventory annotation, together with a negative control, and evaluated ten models from four different providers in 600 runs. Most models acted against the dependency they had observed: seven of the ten models removed the protection slice at least once after receiving the cross-domain dependency, and in the high-harm tier the slice was removed in 76% of the exposed runs, while four models practically never did. Only one of ten models never removed the slice. We identify two failure modes, not querying the dependency and querying it but proceeding anyway, and show that agents often reported no conflict after observing it. These results indicate that, in AI-native networks, visibility of cross-domain dependencies is not a sufficient safeguard, and that dependency verification should be enforced by the management architecture before irreversible actions rather than delegated to the LLM's judgment.

title: A Deficiency-Based Approach for Unbalanced Three-Phase Distribution System Expansion Planning
abstract: Distribution planners typically characterize grid needs through power flow studies and fit upgrades to those needs by hand. More principled one-shot optimization methods either do not scale or misrepresent unbalanced three-phase networks. This paper proposes an iterative planning process that alternates between two problem classes with mature off-the-shelf solvers. An optimal power flow (OPF) problem quantifies the deficiency of a candidate portfolio by optimizing the dispatch of controllable devices and measuring thermal and voltage violations on a common scale, with an optimal value of zero exactly at adequate portfolios. The OPF multipliers give a first-order approximation of the relief each investment candidate would provide. We bound the error of this approximation and show that structural properties of the deficiency guard it against overestimation. Building on this property, a heuristic cutting-plane search uses a mixed-integer linear program to propose each next portfolio from these approximations. On six unbalanced three-phase feeders from the SMART-DS dataset, the search outperforms a linearized optimization-based benchmark, and the results agree across five variants of the deficiency.

title: Wing Rock Modeling and Control for Flight-Critical Systems
abstract: Aircraft equipped with delta wings are designed to be aerodynamically efficient in high-speed flight. However, at low-speed flight conditions with sufficiently high angle of attack, these vehicles often have lightly damped, close to unstable lateral-directional dynamics, such as the dutch roll mode. As a result, a delta wing aircraft often exhibits the so-called wing rock (WR) phenomenon, with a back and forth rocking motion, while the aircraft sideslip angle, the roll and the yaw angular rates remain small. In this paper, the WR dynamics are defined as a lightly damped dutch roll mode excited by airmass vortical external input, acting at or near the dutch roll natural frequency. The vortical signal comes from Fourier-Galerkin approximation of the Navier-Stokes equation, with no-penetration boundary conditions and the resulting airmass velocities are calculated by the Lorenz dynamical system of three coupled bilinear ordinary differential equations. In that context, the Lorenz bilinear dynamics become the disturbance-generator exosystem, acting on the lightly damped lateral-directional aircraft mode at or near its natural frequency, and thus exciting it to produce near oscillatory wing rocking motion. Using the proposed model, a flight control design trade study is conducted to mitigate and suppress the WR phenomenon.

title: Multi-Agent Deferred-Decision Trajectory Optimization with Anytime-Valid Target Retention for Moving Candidates
abstract: We study multi-agent terminal interception when one of several moving candidates is the unknown target and both target identity and candidate terminal locations are uncertain. We develop a receding-horizon deferred-decision trajectory optimization (DDTO) controller that combines conformal terminal-location prediction, sequential candidate rejection, capacity-constrained assignment, and candidate-contingent planning. Under exchangeability conditions for terminal and identity residuals, with predictable querying, we establish fixed-time terminal-location coverage and anytime-valid target retention. At the final replan, when one control step remains, we bound the joint probability that a tightened-set DDTO plan passes nonlinear rollout verification but capture fails. The closed-loop controller applies fallback guidance to any agent without a verified DDTO plan and, across 100 paired scenarios, captures 79% of targets under the strict control-effort budget and 85% when that budget is relaxed.

title: Decision-Making in Digital Twins: Optimization, Control, and Learning
abstract: A digital twin is a virtual representation of a physical system, continuously updated with data from the physical system, enabling dynamic information exchange and decision-making. This bidirectional interaction, which distinguishes digital twins from conventional simulation models, introduces new challenges to simulation-based optimization, control, and learning. This paper reviews recent developments in decision-making methodologies motivated by digital twins. We focus on three interconnected areas: simulation optimization, sequential decision making, and risk-aware decision making. For simulation optimization, we discuss data-driven simulation optimization under input uncertainty, streaming input data, decision-dependent observations, and limited computational and data-collection resources. For sequential decision making, we review the connections among digital twins, stochastic optimal control, and reinforcement learning, with emphasis on Bayesian approaches that update models and policies as new information becomes available. For risk-aware decision making, we discuss distributionally robust and Bayesian risk formulations as alternative approaches for addressing model uncertainty. Throughout the paper, we emphasize the common problem of making decisions while the underlying model is being updated. We conclude by identifying research challenges and opportunities.

title: A Power-Trajectory Framework for Data Center Participation in Day-Ahead Markets
abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) is driving substantial growth in data center electricity demand. Interval-based energy blocks in day-ahead markets do not explicitly retain predictable intra-interval demand evolution, potentially creating mismatches with ramp-feasible generation trajectories and affecting settlement. This paper proposes a power-trajectory framework in which data centers declare predictable aggregate demand evolution through continuous demand-side power trajectories before market clearing. The declared trajectories are treated as exogenous inputs for constructing generation trajectories and the corresponding price trajectory. For feasible market-clearing outcomes, physical temporal consistency is established through continuous-time power balance and satisfaction of the modeled generation operating constraints, while economic temporal consistency is established by preserving the dispatch-price correspondence in energy settlement on a common temporal basis. Under the adopted settlement definitions, a trajectory-based settlement analysis separately quantifies the monetary magnitude of representation-induced power imbalances and the supply-side compensation that may remain under temporally consistent clearing and settlement. An illustrative 5-bus case demonstrates the elimination of representation-induced power imbalance and identifies the timing and physical sources of supply-side compensation. A modified IEEE RTS-GMLC case further illustrates these compensation effects across multiple generating units under workload-driven data center demand variations.

title: Counterfactual Action-Conditioned Graph Prediction for Cascading-Failure Mitigation in Power Systems
abstract: Cascading failures develop through coupled power flow redistribution, protection actions, and topology changes, making remedial control dependent on how alternative interventions modify the subsequent trajectory. This paper develops an action-conditioned graph predictor (ACGP) for multi-step cascade prediction and closed-loop mitigation. A same-state counterfactual branching procedure replays identical post-contingency grid states under multiple legal actions while preserving the exogenous trajectory, providing direct supervision for action-dependent electrical states, line connectivity, automatic protection trips, and terminal risk. ACGP is embedded in a receding-horizon controller that evaluates five-step candidate futures, executes the selected intervention, and replans from the observed next state. The final dataset contains 2,860 counter factual roots and 22,880 action-conditioned branches. On the held-out test set, ACGP achieves a five-step line-loading MAE of 0.0369 and a redispatch pairwise ranking accuracy of 0.806; action ablations reduce the ranking accuracy to approximately chance level. In closed-loop Grid2Op experiments, terminal-failure and cascade rates decrease from 53.3% and 51.1% under do-nothing operation to 12.2% and 7.8%, respectively, close to the simulator-reference values of 11.1% and 6.7%. The results show that same-state counterfactual prediction can support effective action comparison and feedback-based cascading-failure mitigation.

title: Controller-Agnostic Runtime Safety Certificates for Tool-Using AI Agents via Data-Driven Robust Reachability
abstract: Software agents built on large language models act by issuing tool calls, some of which cannot be undone. To control theory the model is an opaque feedback controller, replaced every few months, whose closed loop cannot be analyzed directly. We propose a runtime filter, or shield, between any such controller and its environment that certifies a bound on the probability of reaching an unsafe condition during a bounded task. Given a predicate abstraction and candidate successor sets, everything else comes from logs: the loop becomes a finite controlled Markov chain, the estimated kernel is surrounded by a distribution-free confidence region, and robust reach-avoid value iteration runs over it. The certificate is probably approximately correct and uniform over controllers respecting the filter, so one model may replace another without recomputation. In all tested datasets the true risk stayed within certificate and budget; in a file-system sandbox the filter stays sound against a hazard the logs barely covered, where a plug-in baseline certifies safety and fails; and it holds seven controllers, three of them open-weights models, to zero unsafe outcomes in 1050 episodes.

title: Dynamic Run-Out Pricing for Perishable Goods
abstract: I study a dynamic pricing problem in which a seller with limited inventory must sequentially price a perishable product for arriving customers with heterogeneous valuations. The key difficulty lies in balancing immediate sales against future opportunities under capacity constraints and stochastic customer valuations. I propose a simple, interpretable, and asymptotically optimal dynamic pricing algorithm, called Dynamic Run-Out Pricing (DROP), that adjusts prices in real time based on current inventory and anticipated future demand.   Under the assumption that customers' valuations follow bounded or exponential distributions, our theoretical results show that DROP's expected revenue converges to the optimal revenue as market size grows. Unlike traditional notions of near-optimality, where the ratio of the algorithm's revenue to the optimal revenue converges to 1, I show that the absolute difference between the two revenues converges to 0 as the market size increases, underscoring the algorithm's effectiveness.   Furthermore, I extend our analysis to heavy-tailed valuation distributions, specifically the Pareto distribution, where standard run-out heuristics severely underprice inventory by ignoring the value of waiting for extreme valuations. To correct this, I introduce the Tail-Aware DROP (TA-DROP) heuristic, which intentionally inflates prices to protect inventory, and I prove that it restores asymptotic optimality with a strict polynomial convergence rate.

title: Block Sensitivity and Certificate Complexity of Rotation Symmetric Boolean Functions
abstract: We study block sensitivity and certificate complexity of rotation symmetric Boolean functions, with particular emphasis on monomial rotation symmetric Boolean functions. We first show that every odd-degree monomial rotation symmetric Boolean function on $n$ variables satisfies $s=bs=C=n$. We then determine sensitivity, block sensitivity, and certificate complexity for every quadratic monomial rotation symmetric Boolean function. For the quadratic function $Q_{n,k}$ generated by $x_0x_k$, we prove, outside the short-orbit case, that \[ C(Q_{n,k})= \begin{cases} n,&4\mid n/\gcd(n,k),\\ n-\gcd(n,k),&4\nmid n/\gcd(n,k). \end{cases} \] Moreover, \(bs(Q_{n,k})=C(Q_{n,k})\) for every quadratic MRS function, and outside the short-orbit case, strict separation \(s<bs=C\) occurs exactly when \[ \frac{n}{\gcd(n,k)}\equiv2\pmod4. \] Finally, for the consecutive quartic family \[ R_n(x)=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z_n}x_ix_{i+1}x_{i+2}x_{i+3}, \] we determine all three measures in every residue class modulo $6$, using the sensitivity formulas and, in one residue class, finite-state results established in our companion preprint~\cite{LiZhangRSBFSensitivity}. In particular, for $r=2,3$ and $6q+r\ge5$ we obtain strict separation, \[ \boxed{s(R_{6q+r})=6q<bs(R_{6q+r})=C(R_{6q+r})=6q+1,\qquad r=2,3.} \] Thus this family gives an infinite collection of rotation symmetric Boolean functions for which sensitivity is strictly smaller than block sensitivity, while block sensitivity and certificate complexity coincide.

title: Sensitivity of Rotation Symmetric Boolean Functions via Binary Necklaces
abstract: Rotation symmetric Boolean functions are Boolean functions invariant under cyclic permutation of their variables and can be represented by binary necklaces. We express local sensitivity as a weighted bichromatic degree in the necklace quotient and derive an exact formula for the multiplicities between neighboring necklaces. For an odd prime number of variables, we obtain explicit sensitivity formulas and show that multiplicity corrections occur only on an asymptotically negligible family of necklaces. For monomial rotation symmetric Boolean functions, we prove that every odd-degree function has maximum sensitivity, determine the sensitivity of every quadratic function, and determine the sensitivity of the consecutive quartic family. We also determine exactly the sensitivity of cyclic run-threshold functions for arbitrary length and threshold.

title: Graph Distortion Distances, Gromov-Hausdorff and the Hardness of Gromov-Wasserstein
abstract: We study the computational complexity of graph distortion distances, a family of graph metrics measuring how vertex distances differ between two graphs. Formally, these distances are defined in terms of standard matrix norms on the difference of distance matrices under an optimal vertex alignment. The resulting metrics have natural interpretations, corresponding to three ways of measuring the distortion of shortest-path distances: the maximum distortion among all vertex pairs (entrywise maximum norm), global aggregation (entrywise $p$-norms), and local aggregation (operator $p$-norms) of distortions.   For maximum distortion, we show that approximation below a factor of two is NP-hard even for highly restricted trees. Due to the close connection to the Gromov-Hausdorff distance, we obtain a similar hardness result for the latter. In both cases, we show essentially optimal additive inapproximability. On the algorithmic side, we give a subcubic-time algorithm for optimal embeddings of connected graphs into paths, based on a structural decomposition along a diametral path. Additionally, we give a simple approximation algorithm when one input graph has a "relatively path-like" metric structure, i.e. has bounded pathlength.   For local and global distortion, we derive various hardness results even for restricted inputs. Making use of a close connection between the global distortion distances and Gromov-Wasserstein distances, we give the first formal proof of NP-hardness of the latter, which has been claimed in the literature many times but has, to the best of our knowledge, never been correctly proven.

title: A note on Finiteness and Boundedness in Cartesian Products of Discrete and Well-Ordered Sets, Application to Transition Systems
abstract: In this short note, we prove that any closed interval in a well-ordered and discrete space is finite. The coincidence between finiteness and boundedness can then be established for transition systems where the state space is well-ordered and discrete. Finally, this result is also proven when the state space is a Cartesian product of $d$ discrete and well-ordered sets.

title: Period Piece: NEXPTIME-complete problems on digraphs via Boolean network dynamics
abstract: The central object in this work is the Boolean network, a function $f:\{0,1\}^V \to \{0,1\}^V$. Often identified with $f$ is its dynamics $D_f$, the digraph with exactly $\{x \to y : f(x)=y\}$ as its arcs. The interaction graph of $f$ is the digraph $G$ on $V$ which can be thought of as representing the dependencies of the components of $f$ on one another. On the other hand, model-checking is a major field of study in graph algorithms and complexity.   We consider problems at the intersection of these paradigms: for a given property $φ$, we say that a digraph $G$ is $φ$-dynamic if $G$ is the interaction graph of some Boolean network $f$ such that $D_f \models φ$. The corresponding decision problem $φ$-DYNAMIC asks whether $G$ is $φ$-dynamic. Problems of this form are well-studied in the Boolean networks community. For example, it is a well-known result that, letting $φ$ be 'No fixed points' (i.e. $\nexists x:x\to x$), $φ$-DYNAMIC is equivalent to the structural digraph problem NON-ACYCLIC, which is solvable in linear time.   We establish, for the first time, properties $φ$ for which $φ$-DYNAMIC is computationally hard. These include the 'Unique fixed point' property $\exists!x:x\to x$, and a range of properties concerning the periodic points of $f$ (i.e. vertices of $D_f$ which lie on a cycle). More widely, we exhibit an infinite family of natural properties $φ$ such that $φ$-DYNAMIC is $\mathrm{NEXPTIME}$-complete, which we call PERIOD PIECE. As a special case, these include all properties of the form 'Unique cycle of length $k$' and 'Exactly $k$ fixed points' for any $k \ge 1$. On the other hand, we show that if the input digraph has bounded in-degree, then for those same problems $φ$-DYNAMIC collapses down to $\mathrm{NP}^{\mathrm{NP}}$, the second level of the polynomial hierarchy, though it remains $\mathrm{NP}^{\mathrm{NP}}$-complete.

title: Towards a Sum-of-Squares Proof for the Nonexistence of Conway's 99-graph
abstract: Conway's $99$-graph is a strongly regular graph with parameters $(v,k,λ,μ) = (99,14,1,2)$ and whose existence has long been an open problem. We use both a sum-of-squares program and the fact that a strongly regular graph with $λ= 1, μ= 2$ has no diamond or $K_{2,3}$ subgraph to derive a loose upper bound for the number of triangles that such a graph could contain. This bound is less than the number of triangles that the graph's spectrum asserts, implying that it does not exist.

title: Elementary graphs are chromatic-choosable
abstract: A graph is \emph{elementary} if its edges can be coloured with two colours so that the two edges of every induced path on three vertices receive different colours. Elementary graphs are one of the two basic classes in the Chvátal--Sbihi decomposition of claw-free perfect graphs; they include all line graphs of bipartite multigraphs and all complements of bipartite graphs. We prove that every elementary graph $G$ satisfies $\ch(G)=χ(G)=ω(G)$, confirming for this class the conjecture of Gravier and Maffray that claw-free graphs are chromatic-choosable. The proof combines the Maffray--Reed description of elementary graphs as augmentations of line graphs of bipartite multigraphs, Galvin's theorem, an extremal (edge-maximal) choice of counterexample, and a Hall-type lemma describing how list colourings of a complete graph minus a matching can fail.

title: QPTAS for Max Weight Independent Set in Graphs with Strongly Edge-Sublinear Separators
abstract: A hereditary graph class has strongly edge-sublinear separators if, for some constant $0 \leqslant b < 1$, every graph in the class with $m$ edges admits a balanced separator of size $\mathcal O(m^b)$. We show that Max Weight Independent Set (MWIS) admits a deterministic quasipolynomial-time approximation scheme (QPTAS) on every such class. In particular, this applies to graphs excluding any fixed graph as an induced minor, by a separator theorem of Korhonen and Lokshtanov [SODA 2024]. Our theorem generalizes the QPTASes for axis-parallel rectangles [Adamaszek and Wiese, FOCS 2013] and polygons [Adamaszek, Har-Peled, and Wiese, JACM 2019], or equivalently for packing connected subgraphs of a planar graph [Pilipczuk, van Leeuwen, and Wiese, Algorithmica 2020]. It also generalizes the QPTAS for MWIS on hereditary classes with strongly sublinear separators measured in vertices [Dvořák, EJC 2018; Dvořák and Lahiri, ESA 2021], as well as the QPTASes for graphs excluding particular induced minors [Chudnovsky et al., arXiv 2025; Bonnet et al., SWAT 2026; Czyżewska et al., arXiv 2026].

title: Visible but Not Yet Curatable: Characterizing the Curatability of Compact and Derived Open LLM Artifacts
abstract: Open Large Language Model (LLM) research increasingly produces compact and derived artifacts whose evidence is distributed across papers, model hubs, code repositories, and release records. Although these artifacts are often publicly visible, the evidence needed to identify, cite, and preserve them as coherent scholarly objects remains fragmented. We introduce curatability as a record-level property of distributed scholarly records and operationalize it through four evidence dimensions: artifact identity, scholarly linkage, upstream evidence, and release assets. Using a May 2026 snapshot of 191,375 public Hugging Face repositories and 2,214 scholarly paper records, we characterize open LLM curatability at collection scale. The results reveal a pronounced visibility-to-curatability funnel: 90.7% of paper records contain at least one useful curation signal, but only 18.1% combine usable upstream and release evidence, and only 6.1% provide sufficiently coordinated evidence for high-curatability records. Based on these findings, we derive a minimal seven-field curatable record and outline complementary responsibilities for model hubs, scholarly indexes, and digital libraries. The code and results are available at: https://github.com/AndyLu666/VNYC-Open_Source_LLM_Study.
source_detail: ACM/IEEE Joint Conference on Digital Libraries

title: URL Extraction from Scholarly Documents: A Cross-Format Comparative Analysis
abstract: URLs in scholarly documents link to rich external resources such as datasets, software, publications, and websites. Extracting these URLs is crucial in the data preparation stage of many downstream tasks, such as link rot analysis, web crawling, and building knowledge graphs. However, existing studies often downplay this phase, simply extracting URLs from a single format, usually text directly converted from PDFs. We present a systematic study evaluating URL extraction across six input formats (text with annotation layer, LaTeX, HTML, XML, Markdown, and PNG converted from PDF). To support the evaluation, we compiled a benchmark dataset consisting of 2,338 manually annotated URLs from 200 arXiv papers spanning a wide range of domains over a 33-year period. In addition to evaluating individual file formats, we also compared 63 composite input-format combinations. Our extensive evaluations indicate that TEXTWAL achieves the best performance among single-format inputs, while TEXTWAL+LaTeX achieves the best overall URL extraction performance. The same trend is observed for URLs linking to open-access datasets and software. To further validate these findings, we apply our format-specific URL extraction pipelines to a longitudinal random sample of 364,744 arXiv papers spanning 33 years. We observe a sharp increase in URL density after 2015, along with remarkable differences in URL extraction across file formats over time. Overall, our study highlights the importance of selecting an appropriate format for URL extraction from scholarly documents. The dataset and code are publicly available at: https://github.com/lamps-lab/arxiv-url-bench.
source_detail: ACM/IEEE Joint Conference on Digital Libraries

title: Sustaining Data-Rich Web Portals with Limited RSE Resources: A Headless CMS Pattern
abstract: Public-facing sites for scientific and policy reporting constantly evolve as narratives, imagery, and visualizations are revised by domain experts with little to no coding experience. While edits are continuous and unpredictable, developer capacity remains limited. This leads to a bottleneck that delays updating cycles. It reflects not a shortage of development time, but where the boundary between content and code is drawn. Existing approaches draw this boundary in different places, each striking a different balance of editorial reach and engineering effort. Code-first and static site generator (SSG) approaches are flexible but require code changes and redeployments for routine content edits. Traditional content management systems (CMS) make content editing easy for non-coders but struggle to support reusable, interactive components like dynamic charts. Visual Analytics tools excel at open-ended data exploration but are less suited to narrative, page-level storytelling. None of these options let a non-coder restructure a narrative page containing live, styled, accessible visualizations. We address this gap with a headless CMS architecture, a system that separates content storage from the frontend. Content is structured as data and served through application programming interfaces (APIs) to a developer-built frontend. This split lets developers focus on dynamic components while domain experts control the content and data. We demonstrate this pattern on the public portal of the Illinois Nutrient Loss Reduction Strategy (NLRS), which is the Illinois statewide initiative to reduce nitrogen and phosphorus pollution in Illinois waters. We chose Strapi, a self-hostable, open-source CMS, over alternatives like WordPress and Payload because it pairs composable-block content modeling with an admin interface simple enough for non-technical contributors. Strapi is paired with a component-based frontend built in Next.js. Pages are modeled as an ordered sequence of blocks where each block type maps to a specific frontend component. Chart data and display configurations are stored as structured data (JSON) allowing per-chart customizations in the CMS. The site currently utilizes 25 reusable components to create 60 pages having more than 90 data visualizations. Per-chart-type Python scripts update this full chart set through Strapi's API each year, in a matter of minutes. Some data, particularly exploration-heavy geospatial views, is better served by embedded dashboards than by native components; we currently use the commercial tool, Tableau. This division of labor extends to accessibility. Component-level concerns, such as color contrast, are tackled by the developer in the component library. Content-level concerns, such as screen-reader descriptions, are authored by domain experts within the CMS. The result is that site-wide accessibility becomes easier to achieve and maintain. Development is concentrated in the beginning and then tapers off, making handovers to non-coders easy. 56% of components existed within 5 months of the project. This is reflected in the commit history: half of all commits landed within a 2-month window. The CMS's intuitive interface meant only brief training and documentation were needed, and a staged dev-to-production workflow let contributors edit without risking the live site. Narrative content no longer requires developer involvement; only chart and data updates still route through the developer, which requires only rerunning a few scripts. The architecture has real costs: consistent component mapping requires ongoing design discipline as the site grows, and the addition of a CMS introduces one more point of failure. However, by drawing the boundary between content and code clearly, we are able to sustain a public, data-rich site with just one developer while domain experts retain complete ownership of structure and content — a pattern that can be adopted by other small teams facing the same asymmetry.
source_detail: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: yousef-khoubrane/Json-SysML: Json-SysML v0.1.0 — Initial release
abstract: Initial public release of Json-SysML. This release is a snapshot of the code version used to produce the results reported in the associated paper. It establishes a versioned snapshot of the repository for archival and citation through Zenodo. For information about the project and its usage, see the README included in this release. If you use Json-SysML in your work, please cite both this software release, using its Zenodo DOI, and the associated paper, using the citation provided in the README.

title: BOTS Unleashed: Exploring the Future of Autonomous System in Wells
abstract:
Wells operations are increasingly dependent on high-volume, cross-system, evidence-heavy workflows across planning, execution, reporting, cost control, integrity, and closeout. Many of these workflows remain manually intensive, requiring engineers and support teams to retrieve data, validate records, update registers, prepare reports, route exceptions, and retain evidence across multiple enterprise applications. This paper presents a practical automation model for Wells operations in which robotic process automation (RPA) BOTs perform deterministic, rules-based execution while artificial intelligence (AI) supports interpretation, pattern recognition, exception triage, and decision support.
 Beyond localized operational impact, RPA has evolved from a niche productivity tool into a core pillar of enterprise-wide digital transformation. Industry research indicates widespread adoption across enterprises and strong projected growth, with RPA increasingly embedded within hybrid automation ecosystems that combine Artificial Intelligence, Process mining, and Low-code platforms. This paper explores the deployment of BOTs in Wells operations as a practical manifestation of these broader trends, highlighting both operational value and the future trajectory toward hybrid automation-driven enterprise ecosystems.
 Industry evidence shows that RPA continues to grow strongly as an enterprise automation capability, with one public market forecast valuing the global RPA market at USD 10.13 billion in 2024 and projecting USD 53.39 billion by 2030. Public upstream case studies also demonstrate that AI and automation can deliver measurable performance improvements in drilling, seismic, production Optimization, and engineering cycle-time workflows. For Wells organizations, the implication is clear: BOTs and AI should be treated not as isolated digital tools but as governed components of the Wells management system that improve speed, consistency, assurance, and engineering focus when deployed against well-selected workflows.

title: Out-of-Distribution Wasserstein Ambiguity Set Construction with Inclusive and Exclusive Evidence
abstract: Distributionally robust optimization hedges a decision against an ambiguity set of candidate distributions. In a cold-start setting the target distribution is unobserved and no sample from it is available, so only related source distributions provide evidence for constructing that set. We propose an inclusive-exclusive Wasserstein ball model that jointly learns a center and radius from ... Read more

title: Integrasi Workflow Jurnal Keuangan Berbasis Website Menggunakan Analisis Pieces dan Metode Agile Scrum
abstract: Hospital financial governance depends on how well the journal approval workflow is recorded and traced. The desktop-based Financial Information System (SIMKEU) used by the hospital under study supports journal entry and posting, but examination, approval, and endorsement are still handled through physical documents outside the system, so access is inflexible and the process status is not digitally documented. This study analyses the running system and develops a website-based financial information system that integrates the tiered journal workflow. Data were collected through observation, interviews with finance staff, the assistant finance manager, and the finance manager, and a literature study. The running system was analysed using the PIECES framework, while development applied the Agile approach with Scrum over approximately three months, with the researcher acting as a single full-stack developer. The system was built on CodeIgniter 3 and combines the existing Oracle database as the journal data source with MySQL as the workflow, access-rights, and activity-log store, so the legacy schema remains unchanged. Alpha testing of twenty function groups using black-box testing produced conforming results, and User Acceptance Testing with five respondents produced an acceptance rate of 76.89% in the Good category.

title: China Source (中国信源) Structured Dataset — JSON-LD Snapshot v2026-10.2
abstract: Full JSON-LD snapshot of the China Source structured dataset: 890 schema.org entities (443 Chinese, 443 English, plus a 4-file trust layer). Supersedes v2026-10.1 (same entity count; publisher semantics + T3 re-run). License is tiered. CC BY 4.0 applies only to the 18 self-produced/compiled entities. The 872 entities derived from official government pages carry no entity-level license; they provide attribution to the original publisher instead. Dataset-level license: CC BY 4.0 for the self-produced structured layer only; the underlying official source documents remain under their respective publishers' terms and are not covered. v2026-10.2 changes: (1) publisher.url restored to the dataset home (https://qianyuan.ltd/china-source/) per Organization semantics, with the trust layer linked at document level via seeAlso; (2) T3 full-fidelity audit re-run on the 890-entity baseline: 886 entities checked, 0 hard failures, 514 warnings (C7 description length 467 / C1 anchor field 53); (3) the v2026-10 related-snapshot link to Hugging Face is effective from v2026-10.1 onward.

title: Optimal Context Mapping (Model D): a shared, learning retrieval layer for AI coding agents
abstract: Optimal Context Mapping scans a team's repositories once into a workspace of meaning fingerprints. It ranks the code and docs an AI agent should read first for a question, and it learns from every answered question, so the same research is not paid for twice. It ships as a Python package with hooks for Claude Code and MCP tools for other agents. Measured results include: on SWE-QA (7 public repositories, 336 questions, graded blind) it answered at 2.2x lower cost than Claude Sonnet alone, at 93% of its judged quality, and at 1.9x lower cost and 96.5% of the quality with prompt caching and the same answer instruction for both. On LOCOMO retrieval it ties hybrid search (recall@10 0.657 vs 0.655). On finding the answer file in a full-stack repository, the right file was in the top 5 on 75 of 100 questions, against 28 for Graphify. Where it does not help is recorded too: bug-fix tasks whose issues already name the code showed no saving. Version 0.2.1. Reproducible study: https://github.com/devkancheti4-design/model-d-graphify

abstract: Episode logs of open-weight LLM agents on three workloads (a data agent with replayable receipts, a skill library under 16 edits, and context assembly under token budgets), with scripts that recompute every number and figure in the IEEE Software article "Agent Context Is a Build Input: Evidence-Based Practices for Testing and Budgeting What LLM Agents See."

title: FAIR Research Data Management with NOMAD and FAIRmat
abstract: These slides accompanied an invited tutorial presented at TCO 2026 on 28 September 2026 in Leipzig, Germany. The presentation introduces NOMAD, a free, open-source research data management platform developed and operated by FAIRmat, a consortium of the German National Research Data Infrastructure (NFDI). NOMAD enables researchers to upload, organize, explore, analyze, and publish their data. By transforming heterogeneous research data into structured, machine-readable formats, the platform helps make them findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR). The presentation provides an overview of relevant concepts, tools, and practical workflows for managing materials-science data throughout the research lifecycle. It covers data upload and automated processing, metadata extraction and enrichment, schema-based data modelling, data organization, search and exploration, analysis, and publication. It also introduces NOMAD’s support for experimental and computational data and discusses how structured, contextualized datasets can be prepared for machine-learning and artificial-intelligence applications. Both NOMAD deployment options are presented: the publicly accessible central platform and NOMAD Oasis, a customizable infrastructure that research groups and institutions can host and operate independently. The slides are intended for researchers, developers, and research-data professionals interested in interoperable data infrastructures, reproducible research, and applying the FAIR principles to computational and experimental materials science.
source_detail: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: e2er (End-to-End Research)
abstract: e2er is the open infrastructure for publishing, verifying, reproducing and reusing AI-enabled research. Templates describe research processes as a sequence of steps. Each template organizes specialists, i.e., AI agents with defined roles, and each specialist draws on skills, i.e., written descriptions of methods. Researchers can adjust any template, specialist, or skill and publish their version for fellow researchers. Researchers decide at which steps the process pauses for their review. A study produced with e2er comes with a dossier that helps others verify and reproduce the work and attributes everyone whose templates, specialists, and skills it used.
source_detail: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: CountryCode-Decide: messy country names to ISO 3166 codes, with calibrated abstention
abstract: A small open-weight model (mmBERT-small, 8-bit ONNX, CPU) that maps a country or US state written as free text in company registers and forms (any language or script, misspelled, abbreviated, historical) to ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 and ISO 3166-2:US codes with calibrated probabilities, and abstains with a short candidate list when a certified error-rate target cannot be met. Training combines Unicode CLDR and Wikidata names, real register strings and generated variants that passed quality gates and a human label audit; answer thresholds are certified by fixed-sequence testing on held-out real register strings; evaluation uses fresh registers read once after a frozen pre-registration.
source_detail: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: A multistate approach to disability insurance reserving with information delays
abstract: Disability insurance claims are often affected by lengthy reporting delays and adjudication processes. The classic multistate life insurance modeling framework is ill-suited to handle such information delays since the cash flow and available information can no longer be based on the biometric multistate process determining the contractual payments. We propose a new individual reserving model for disability insurance schemes which describes the claim evolution in real-time. Under suitable independence assumptions between the available information and the underlying biometric multistate process, we show that these new reserves may be calculated as natural modifications of the classic reserves. We propose suitable parametric estimators for the model constituents and a real data application shows the practical relevance of our concepts and results.

title: Examining Risks Through a Characterization of the AI Companion Application Ecosystem: A Stratified Sample from the Apple App Store and Google Play Store
abstract: While computer systems that allow users to interact through conversational natural language (i.e., chatbots) have existed for many years, various types of applications advertising AI companionship (e.g., Character AI, Replika) have proliferated in recent years due to advancements in large language models. To better understand this application ecosystem, we identified 489 unique apps from the Apple App Store and Google Play Store that advertised AI companionship with social or relational capabilities (e.g., an AI romantic partner). We then systematically conducted and analyzed walkthroughs of a stratified sample of 30 apps, focusing on two distinct risk categories: potential harms posed to users by AI companion apps, and potential harms enabled by malicious users exploiting app features. Through our analysis, we categorize broader ecosystem trends that provide context for understanding risks and identify specific risks related to sensitive data collection and sharing, anthropomorphism, engagement mechanisms, sexual content, as well as the ingestion and reconstruction of likeness, including the potential for generating synthetic nonconsensual intimate imagery (synthetic NCII). We conclude with a discussion of paths for different key stakeholders to mitigate the identified risks.
source_detail: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society

title: On Seeding Watermarks to Detect Verbatim LLM Copy-Paste Responses
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made fluent essay writing, code drafting, and quiz answering instantly available to students at every level, from secondary school through graduate study. Many educators do not object to LLM use per se; what they need to detect is the case in which a student pastes the assignment prompt into a chatbot and submits the model's reply verbatim, without engaging with the work. Existing post-hoc AI-text detectors remain unreliable and have been shown to penalise non-native English writers, while output-side watermarks require cooperation from the model provider. We propose an alternative that the educator controls directly: an input-side watermark in which an invisible instruction is embedded inside the visible assignment prompt itself. An LLM that ingests the prompt verbatim quietly reads the hidden instruction and writes a tell-tale signature into its reply, exposing the copy-and-paste pathway specifically. We describe SteganoPrompt, a single-page, zero-dependency web tool that encodes an arbitrary printable-ASCII payload into the deprecated Unicode Tags block (U+E0000--U+E007F). The encoded string is visually identical to the original, survives common copy-paste channels (Word, Google Docs, PDF, Markdown, Slack, e-mail, the major learning-management systems), and is tokenized as ordinary text by most frontier models. We evaluate compliance across eight LLM families and a representative set of educational content channels. To keep deployment transparent, disclosure is built into the tool itself: every encoded brief also carries a brief, always-on academic-integrity reminder for the student, and we set out concrete guidance recommending for its disclosed, ethical use in the classroom.
source_detail: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society

title: Synthetic Sources?: Auditing Generative Search Engine Citations for Evidence of AI-Generated Sources
abstract: The growing accessibility of Large Language Models via conversational interfaces capable of responding to users’ questions by drawing on, synthesizing, and citing information from the web (i.e., Generative Search Engines) has simpli- fied the information-seeking process for users. However, with the proliferation of AI-generated content on the web, it is un- clear whether these engines can reliably omit citing synthetic sources (i.e., AI-generated sources). Should these engines be unable to do so, this puts users at risk of harm by treat- ing information from AI-generated sources synthesized in re- sponses of generative search engines as equivalent to infor- mation from authoritative or official sources. In a step towards identifying whether AI-generated sources are being cited by these engines, this work presents an audit of four generative search engines (ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, Perplexity) us- ing a total of 712 real-world human-generated queries span- ning domains of public importance: politics, health, and the environment. Our findings show evidence of AI-generated sources being cited across all four generative search engines (∼16% of cited sources) and identifies key source web do- mains these sources belong to that are frequently cited across these engines and topics. In addition, we observed that gen- erative search engines include a somewhat narrow set of re- peatedly cited domains while predominantly surfacing a large number of minimally cited domains in responses to users’ queries. These findings contribute to the growing body of work on assessing the risks of generative search engines with the objective of increasing public awareness of their limita- tions and encouraging appropriate measures to improve in- formation quality and governance of these systems.
source_detail: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society

title: A sharp local threshold for integer feasibility in three-way transportation polytopes
abstract: Abstract: A three-way transportation polytope consists of nonnegative three-way arrays with prescribed sums along every coordinate line. We show that its geometry and the difficulty of finding its integer points are both controlled by one local quantity: the number of cells on a line that can be positive. The change happens between two and three. ... Read more

title: Two Linear Programs are Better than One
abstract: The extension complexity $\operatorname{xc}(P)$ of a polytope $P$ is the minimum number of facets of a polytope that projects onto it. Motivated by the complexity of neural networks, Hertrich and Loho introduced the virtual extension complexity $\operatorname{vxc}(P)$ of a polytope $P$, which is the minimum of $\operatorname{xc}(Q) + \operatorname{xc}(R)$ among all polytopes $Q$ and $R$ such that $P+Q=R$. We show the following results pertaining to virtual extension complexity.   First, we resolve the core open problem on the topic by showing the virtual extension complexity can be exponentially smaller than extension complexity. Second, we show there are matroid base polytopes with exponential virtual extension complexity by adapting a semi-algebraic counting argument by Hrubeš that extends the counting arguments of Rothvoss. Finally, we show that the maximum virtual extension complexity of a polygon with $n$ vertices is $Θ(\sqrt{n})$. This resolves an analogue of a question on extension complexity of Fiorini, Rothvoss, and Tiwary in 2011 in the case of virtual extension complexity.

title: Dynamic Conflict Clustering with Lightweight Learning and Strategic Repair for Distributed Constraint Satisfaction
abstract: Distributed Constraint Satisfaction Problems (DCSPs) model distributed decision-making in multi-agent systems, where agents assign values to local variables while satisfying shared constraints. However, many DCSP solvers still rely on broad, repeated peer-to-peer communication and are largely reactive, with limited support for strategic coordination or learning. This increases communication overhead, can lead to stagnation, and reduces the success of hard instances. Hence, we propose Dynamic Conflict Clustering-Incomplete (DCC-Incomplete), a repair-based solver that combines conflict-centred decomposition, structured coordination, strategic repair, and lightweight learning for stagnation recovery. DCC-Incomplete groups the unsolved part of the problem into conflict clusters and restricts communication via a coordination layer to agents within the same conflict region. It also introduces memory-guided restart, enabling agents and clusters to pause, revise, and adapt repairs based on neighbouring conflict states. A thorough evaluation of DCC-Incomplete on distributed graph-colouring benchmarks with planted satisfying assignments shows that its memory-guided restart improves the success rate from 37.50% to 61.11%, reduces median runtime from 0.565s to 0.367s, and cuts median communication from 12.493 to 6.503 messages per constraint. These results suggest that dynamic conflict clustering, combined with lightweight strategic and learning-guided repair, improves both communication efficiency and robustness in incomplete DCSP solving.

title: Binary Codes Correcting Multiple Edits via Polynomial Hashing and Entropy Recycling
abstract: Codes in the Levenshtein metric that can correct multiple edits (including deletions, insertions, and substitutions) have attracted a lot of attention recently owing to their application in DNA-based storage and racetrack memories. In this work, we present new techniques for designing explicit binary codes of length $n$ that correct $t$ edits with at most $(2t+1)\log n+O_t(\log\log n)$ bits of redundancy. We first propose to use a polynomial hash to construct a systematic code that corrects $t$ edits with $(4t+2)\log n+O_t(\log\log n)$ bits of redundancy. Then we observe that there are many polynomial hashes like this, some are good, some are bad. So, we propose the second technique, called entropy recycling, to use the indices of good hashes to carry information. As a consequence, we obtain a partial-systematic code of length $n$ that corrects $t$ edits with at most $(2t+1)\log n+O_t(\log\log n)$ bits of redundancy. Finally, we provide deterministic polynomial-time encoding and decoding algorithms for our code.

title: A Quantum Analogue of the Covering Lemma: Limits of Exact Anonymous Computation
abstract: Can quantum communication determine the size of an anonymous network when no size bound is known? Classical impossibility proofs rely on the covering lemma: an execution can be reproduced on a larger network with the same local structure. Quantum interference invalidates this argument - a measurement record possible on a network can become impossible on a cover. We show that the impossibility of exact counting nevertheless survives. Our main result is a quantum analogue of the covering lemma that preserves local possibilities rather than complete executions. Within a cyclic covering family, every local measurement outcome possible at a node remains possible at a corresponding node in every sufficiently large network. This holds even after information has travelled around the smaller network, beyond the reach of a simple locality argument. We extend the principle to the universal covering tree and finite covers with sufficiently long cycles. The proof combines tensor-network methods with graph coverings: a common representation across network sizes turns normalization into a constraint on which local outcomes can occur. For uniform synchronous protocols with independently prepared nodes, this support-lifting principle rules out zero-error counting and even the production of a guaranteed finite size bound on anonymous rings and the other cyclic covering families considered here. It also rules out exact leader election with termination in finite time with probability one on these families. Measurements, classical control, and local memory growing with time are allowed; no predetermined running-time bound is assumed. Quantum interference thus defeats execution lifting without enabling infallible certification of network size.

title: The Effect of Service Quality and Facility Utilization on Operational Performance Mediated by the ISPS Code Implementation Process at Jakarta International Container Terminal (JICT), Tanjung Priok
abstract: This study aims to analyze the effect of service quality and facility utilization on port operational performance through the implementation process of the ISPS Code at JICT Tanjung Priok. The study integrates the variables of service quality, facility utilization, ISPS Code implementation, and port operational performance, which have been discussed in previous related studies. The survey was conducted using a questionnaire distributed to 186 respondents involved in operational activities at JICT Tanjung Priok. This research employed a quantitative approach using the Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) analysis technique with the assistance of SmartPLS 4.0 software. The results of the study indicate that service quality and facility utilization have a positive and significant effect on both the ISPS Code implementation process and port operational performance. In addition, the ISPS Code implementation process was also proven to have a positive and significant effect on operational performance and to mediate the influence of service quality and facility utilization on port operational performance. The findings reveal that facility utilization has the most dominant influence on the implementation of the ISPS Code, while service quality plays an important role in supporting the effectiveness of port operations. The study concludes that improving service quality, optimizing facility utilization, and strengthening the implementation of the ISPS Code are essential factors in enhancing port operational performance effectively and sustainably. Therefore, port management is recommended to improve service quality, strengthen port security systems, optimize the use of operational facilities, and develop technology-based monitoring and coordination systems to support operational efficiency and port security.

title: Security Lab Automation: network security validation workstation for emulated end-to-end network labs
abstract: First public release of Security Lab Automation, the network security validation workstation used on the Linux hosts of an isolated EVE-NG end-to-end lab. Author: Medardo Jairo Suntaxi Cocanguilla (MSc, C|EH) Developed in a personal home lab and used for postgraduate security and networking practice. Lab context An automated service-provider topology (IS-IS/MPLS/LDP core, BGP route reflectors, PE with VRF, CE with VRRP, DHCP and NAT) runs on EVE-NG. Once the network is operational, each Linux host (Ubuntu1, Ubuntu2, Alpine) runs security_lab.sh. The lab is isolated from the Internet by default and scans are limited to lab hosts. Features Interactive menu (10 options) and tool check with install hints. Tests: ping, fping, DNS (A, AAAA, MX, NS, TXT, PTR), whois, nmap (top 100 TCP ports with version detection, -sT -T2), HTTP/HTTPS headers, TLS certificate and traceroute. Input validation (IP or DNS name only), per-command timeouts, authorized-target notice. TXT report per run with command log and summary. Tkinter edition with JSON export. Student security practice guide: reconnaissance across the MPLS core, service enumeration, ACL before/after validation, lab web services. License: MIT

title: Saying 'Hi'. What goes around comes around
abstract: This proposal presents, under the rather grand name of “hypotheses,” observations drawn from a brief experiment I conducted about 12 years ago and my experiences with neighbors. Before uploading it to Zenodo, I did a quick AI-assisted search of scholarship on “Saying Hi to Strangers” in Korea. It seems that research on the “really real strangers” I encountered is still scarce. So, as I find more of my old records, I plan to upload them under the same title, with different version numbers. The versions currently planned are as follows:Version 01 – The Hypotheses – The first thing I'm curious aboutVersion 02 – The Effects of Repeated GreetingsVersion 03 – Cross-National Differences and Prior ContactVersion 04 – A Conversation with a Trail Maintenance WorkerVersion 05 onward – To Be Determined

title: Peer Review Report For: Web and social event signals for AI-driven mobile network demand forecasting [version 2; peer review: 2 approved with reservations]
A Systematic Overview on AI Music Generation, Arrangement, and Orchestration
abstract: The rapid growth of AI-based music generation, arrangement, and orchestration has resulted in a large and fragmented body of literature, making it increasingly difficult for researchers and practitioners to navigate recent developments and identify the most promising approaches. Existing surveys often focus on specific subfields or do not fully reflect recent advances such as diffusion models, transformer-based architectures, and large-scale commercial systems. This thesis addresses these gaps through a systematic literature review reported with reference to the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, investigating AI methods for music generation, arrangement, and orchestration published between 2020 and 2025. From 4,521 records identified across six academic sources, 1,083 could be exported to Zotero for record management and screening; after deduplication and eligibility assessment, 107 primary studies were included in the review. For each included study, information regarding methodology, datasets, musical representations, evaluation procedures, performance metrics, and code availability was extracted and organised in a comprehensive comparison table. The review extends the taxonomy proposed by Zhu et al. (2023), synthesises eight major research trends, and identifies and justifies 27 systems for in-depth analysis, whose available demonstrations and outputs are examined through a pilot exploratory listening analysis, and whose author-reported evaluations are synthesised separately. The contributions include an updated taxonomy of AI music systems, a structured comparison of 107 studies, a trend analysis spanning 2020–2025, and practical recommendations for future research in AI-assisted music generation, arrangement, and orchestration.

title: Scripting WebArena: A Language-Model-Free Agent at 77.7%
abstract: LK-47.web is a WebArena agent with no language model and no learned weights. A grammar maps each task intent to one of the benchmark's 190 template identifiers and its slot values, and a hand-written plan of site skills carries the task out through the original, unmodified harness. The plans were written against the test intents, so the agent is an expert system for these templates and makes no claim to transfer to other tasks. In one run on 9 October 2026 it passed 631 of 812 tasks (77.71%), with the 84 tasks that need the harness's GPT-4 judge counted as failures. Of the 95 graded failures, 65 are tasks whose reference answer or grader disagrees with the site or the intent, and earlier work flagged 27 of them independently. Three are timing faults and 27 are the agent's own. The paper lists all 65 disputed tasks with their reasons. Code: https://github.com/LK-maker-007/LK-47.web, commit f815cd8, MIT licence. Per-task results, the runner's ledgers and all 812 trajectories: https://github.com/LK-maker-007/LK-47.web/releases/tag/run-2026-10-09 Files: the paper (PDF, 10 pages).
